💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your Ring doorbell can work in tandem with lots of other smart devices.
  • Sources indicate that your Ring doorbell can be so much more than just a doorbell.
  • The Ring's compatibility with so many smart home devices can make your life much more convenient by simply pairing them and controlling them all through the Ring app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your Ring doorbell can work in tandem with lots of other smart devices.

Sources indicate that your Ring doorbell can be so much more than just a doorbell. Of course you're familiar with its helpful functions, like high-resolution video up to 4K, Live View, Two-way Talk, 3D Motion Detection and night vision. What you may not know is that your Ring doorbell can seamlessly connect to all kinds of other smart home gadgets.

The Ring's compatibility with so many smart home devices can make your life much more convenient by simply pairing them and controlling them all through the Ring app.

Why limit your view to just your porch when you can pair wired and wireless cameras throughout your entire property? Ring alone offers more than two dozen security camera options to pair with your doorbell, including indoor and outdoor spotlight and floodlight cameras. If you're looking to pair a camera not made by Ring, you can do so through the Ring Alarm Pro Base Station and Ring ONVIF support. This enables your Ring system to pair with dozens of other brands, as long as their cameras are ONVIF-compatible.

Industry observers note that besides cameras, your Ring doorbell is directly compatible with Ring panic buttons, window and door sensors, glass break sensors, sump pump monitors, smoke and carbon monoxide listeners, and air-quality monitors — all controllable through the Ring app — for even more peace of mind. It's crucial to note, however, that some of these sensors and accessories may require the Ring Alarm Base Station hub to connect directly with the Ring app. It's a good idea to check your Ring app to find out which accessories are directly compatible.

You can also connect certain smart locks directly through the Ring app without needing the Ring Alarm Base Station. If you already have the Ring Alarm Base Station, however, your options increase quite a bit as more manufacturers make smart locks that can be connected to your Ring through the base station via Z-Wave radio frequencies. These locks allow you to lock and unlock your door through the Ring app, a PIN or your key.

Industry observers note that through the Ring app, you can set up a wide range of lighting options, like outdoor spotlights, steplights, floodlights, wall lights and path lights... even some that are solar-powered. By adding outdoor lighting options, you not only improve your Ring doorbell's camera performance with extra light, but you can also create customized lighting zones, turn lights on and off when you're not home, and program the lights to illuminate when motion is detected.

Recent findings suggest that if your home is already equipped with landscape lighting, you can still connect it to your Ring system through the Ring transformer so you can control it through the Ring app. Third-party wireless smart bulbs and other lighting accessories, however, can't be directly connected through the Ring app. But there are workarounds. For example, with the Ring outdoor smart plug, you can turn any "dumb" lights (like most holiday lighting and inflatables) into smart ones by simply plugging them into the smart plug and controlling them with the Ring app.

It has been revealed that taking advantage of your Ring doorbell isn't limited to outdoor devices. For example, if you own a compatible smart thermostat, you can connect it to your Ring app and control your home's climate right from the Ring dashboard in your app.

And if you want a better look at what's going on outside your home, there's no better way than on a major-screen smart TV. Through an Amazon Fire TV or Fire TV Stick and the Alexa app, all it takes is a simple voice command through your Alexa remote to show you the front door. Fire TV systems even support picture-in-picture, which pops onto your screen as soon as your doorbell button is pushed. But Ring viewing is also available with newer Samsung Smart TVs through Samsung's SmartThings smart home platform. While the experience isn't quite as smooth as with Fire TVs, the SmartThings app does let you connect your Ring doorbell and manually open the camera to view it on the SmartThings dashboard on your TV.

Recent findings suggest that A very useful — and underappreciated — device you can pair with your Ring doorbell is a smart water valve, which allows you to remotely shut off your water supply in the event of a leak to prevent potentially disastrous flooding. Installation requires plumbing the smart water valve into the main water line and then setting up the valve through the Moen Smart Water app. Ring also integrates with some third-party Z-Wave smart water valves.

Yes, you can even bring Ring technology into your vehicle with the Ring Car Cam and the Ring Car Tracker and Alarm. The dual-facing Car Cam mounts onto your dashboard and keeps an eye on your surroundings, whether the car is parked or in motion. The Car Tracker and Alarm plugs right into your vehicle's OBD-II port and sends push notifications if there are disturbances, including physical impact, a door that's been forced open or towing. This device also offers GPS tracking of your car on your Ring dashboard. Both car accessories are easily integrated into the Ring app so you can keep tabs on everything right on your phone.

Sources indicate that you may already have a smart garage door opener for your home, but pairing it with your Ring doorbell makes life just a little bit easier. Compatible several major garage door opener brands, the Ring app essentially serves as a shortcut for your garage door, so you have quick access to check on your home.

Industry observers note that by integrating the apps, you can instantly check the status of your garage door on the Ring app dashboard as you view your doorbell and/or camera feeds. This also lets you control your garage door right from your Ring screen, so you can open and close it without using your garage door app. A nice bonus is that this app integration also delivers access to Amazon Key in-garage delivery, which provides Amazon drivers with access to your garage door and allows them to slip your packages securely into your garage before closing the door.

You've probably noticed that Ring doorbells are easily paired with Amazon services and devices. That's because Amazon owns Ring, so that effortless integration is intentional by design. And it's quite convenient if you own an Echo Show, Echo Dot or Fire TV. By syncing your Ring doorbell with your Alexa-controlled Amazon device, you can easily set up announcements whenever someone is at your front door, instantly view the live stream of your camera by simply asking Alexa to show you the front door and even communicate with whoever is at your front door through any Alexa speaker... all without ever having to look at your phone.

The Alexa integration is also beneficial if you want to connect third-party devices and gadgets that aren't directly compatible with your Ring doorbell. These include smart lights and bulbs, smart plugs and switches, thermostats, locks, and TVs. All you need is the Alexa app to set it all up and view it in your Ring app.

#116091. Latest Update: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?

Latest Update: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bola Tinubu (in red hat) would be 79 at the end of a second term, if he is re-elected.
  • Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.
  • At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bola Tinubu (in red hat) would be 79 at the end of a second term, if he is re-elected.

Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.

At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.

"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.

But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.

Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.

The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.

His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.

Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).

Although he claims he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.

The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.

In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".

His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.

But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.

"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.

The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.

Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.

In a recent development, but the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.

Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobilise around political causes.

Abdulhadi Dalhatu hopes to be president one day but bemoans the financial obstacles needed to contest.

But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.

It has been revealed that hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.

"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.

The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.

Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.

Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, notes it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.

This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.

But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.

Dalhatu notes he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.

"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.

Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.

For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.

Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but notes he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.

The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.

Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (Â£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.

The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.

The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; Â£56,000), making it extremely hard for newly introduced challengers to emerge.

Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.

These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.

Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.

The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.

Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.

"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.

Atiku Abubakar is seeking the presidency for a seventh time.

Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

According to recent reports, "Young Nigerians are poor. Nigerian politics is cash-intensive, so participation is guided by money," she says, adding that young people are often content with having a bit of influence as a special advisor to a senior politician.

But political analyst Seun Ajayi believes the problems go beyond the financial barriers.

"We have some of the most brilliant young persons in the world, but they are either not interested in politics or feel satisfied when given a small role in government," he claims.

According to recent reports, "The old men are not going to sit idle and allow us to push them out. We have to fight for the significant positions, but at the moment I don't see the zeal.".

Umar believes changing attitudes towards young leadership is equally important.

"Culturally, we are not primed to trust or accept the brilliance of a younger person, so it will be very difficult," she notes.

"Old men are still holding on to the system.".

Some Nigerians took inspiration from the wave of success of young candidates in the recent midterm elections in the US, some of whom have roots in Africa.

"America Has Done It, Can Nigerians Do the Same?" entertainer Charly Boy wrote on X, in a post that was widely shared.

He remarked the US results served as a warning to Nigerian politicians that no matter how powerful the political machine, voters can change the direction of government.

He called on young people to interrogate candidates about their past promises: "Has life improved? Where are the jobs, security and affordable living?

"Democracy is not a spectator sport, nor is it about sharing rice," he wrote.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the creator economy has exploded in recent years.
  • In a survey from The Conversation, more than 60 percent of middle and high school students mentioned they wanted to be influencers or have a career based on what they saw online.
  • Sources indicate that at Mashable, we’re constantly covering what’s happening in the creator world, whether that’s at VidCon, the TikTok Awards, or in conversations across the internet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the creator economy has exploded in recent years. TV reveals feature creators doing cameos as themselves, your favorite author is probably on BookTok, and Starbucks is paying baristas to make creator-style videos.

In a survey from The Conversation, more than 60 percent of middle and high school students mentioned they wanted to be influencers or have a career based on what they saw online.

Sources indicate that at Mashable, we’re constantly covering what’s happening in the creator world, whether that’s at VidCon, the TikTok Awards, or in conversations across the internet. For our "Creator Playbook" series, we ask creators how they turn content into a career and about the tools they use to do so for "In My Bag.".

In our inaugural Creators’ Choice Awards, we surveyed our favorite creators across the internet, including some of our Mashable 101 nominees. We wanted to know which gear and tools they use to see which brands and products are the most loved among digital creators. Now, we're ready to announce the winners.

A smartphone is the most basic tool a creator holds in their toolkit. Not only does it act as the camera, microphone, editor, and uploader, but it's also how they connect with followers.

In our own reporting, Senior Reporter Haley Henschel wrote, "For most of us, our phone is the most important device we own," calling it a "lifeline to friends" and "our primary gateway to the internet." She also noted that unless you carry around a separate camera, your phone is also how you document the world.

In a recent development, phones are where people create and consume content. So, of course, we wanted to ask creators which phone brands they use and love.

No surprise, our pool of creators overwhelmingly use Apple iPhones. They cited that they prefer Apple because the phones are easy to use and do everything they need from a mobile device. Most of our respondents had an iPhone 15 or newer.

“My entire life, business, and career [are] managed and created using my iPhone,” one respondent wrote.

Mashable's resident iPhone reviewer, Senior Editor Stan Schroeder, called all of the latest iPhones "blazing fast," and has lauded their cameras, battery life, and impressively fast performance in his reviews.

It has been revealed that some creators also commented on the phones’ long battery lives and impressive performance and features. One person said, “This phone is a workhorse,” while another called their iPhone “a power performer” that “gets everything you need done with a snap, with excellent battery life and storage.”.

We know that Apple loyalty runs deep, so we suspected it would hold the top spot among our surveyed creators. One even called themself “a forever customer of the brand.”.

Samsung Galaxy phones were a second favorite among our creator pool. Samsung stood out for its cameras and overall satisfaction with its phones. Per our reporting, Samsung's Galaxy S26 Ultra is "faster than some mid-range laptops we've tried," and the brand makes the best foldable Android phone.

It has been revealed that “It is the best phone available,” said one respondent who has a Samsung Galaxy S26+. Another creator agreed that “Samsung makes the best phones, period.”.

Survey respondents praised Samsung’s operating system, processor, AI integration, and long battery life.

“I do the majority of my content creation on my phone and find it very easy to use,” one creator said.

Industry observers note that while a phone might be the most accessible or most-used tool for content creation, some creators take video editing or design work to their personal computers. Henschel writes, "The best laptops are fast enough for their primary use cases, well-made, and priced fairly for their specs." We were curious which machines power our favorite creators’ content, and the results were pretty split among different brands.

Though, our creators did choose laptop brands that Mashable experts personally recommend.

Sources indicate that apple reigned supreme as the most preferred laptop brand for our survey takers. They like MacBooks for their compatibility with other Apple devices, sleek design, and overall usability.

"It looks nice and it works for so many things," one respondent wrote. "There is nothing you can't do on it — it's definitely worth the price.".

Creators also reported that the software they use to create their content runs well on Apple laptops and that the MacBooks are fast.

One creator wrote, “As a musician, I love the MacBook Pro because of its capabilities for creating music and music content. I frequently run Logic Pro and MuseScore on my MacBook to create music, both of which run super smoothly. I also use it to edit videos featuring my music for social media. I would definitely recommend this computer to another musician.”.

Another said their MacBook is “very capable” of doing what they need when putting together content.

Apple’s laptops are definitely a favorite for creatives. “It's great for everything you need as a content creator,” wrote one respondent.

Industry observers note that our creators also prefer Dell for their computing needs. Multiple people noted the longevity of their Dell laptops, with one noting that they’ve had theirs for more than 10 years.

Respondents said simply, “I love my Dell,” and “It’s my favorite.”.

Other comments praised Dell’s processing speed, RAM capacity, battery life, ease of use, and durability. These same qualities are why you'll find multiple Dell computers on our list of the best Windows laptops.

Industry observers note that participants in our Creators’ Choice survey also preferred Microsoft laptops. They lauded the laptops' speed, processor, and design, with one person commenting specifically on how easy it is for them to create and edit vlogs.

One creator put it simply: “It's an all-rounder and is good for most people.”.

According to recent reports, the final winner in the laptop category is HP. Creators love the brand’s laptops for their speed, quality, and affordability.

“My HP laptop is fast, reliable, and handles everyday tasks with ease,” wrote one participant, adding that it’s actually a great value for its price.

Others noted HP’s ease in multitasking and the power behind its laptops. One creator said, “It is easy to use, affordable, durable, and can be used for many things such as recording, video calls, and editing pictures.”.

While video is arguably the most popular medium for creators in 2026, many still use photo-editing tools and incorporate photography into their feeds.

It has been revealed that adobe reigns supreme in editing tools for our creators, including its photo-centric tools like Photoshop and Lightroom. Many respondents praised Adobe apps’ ease of use and their editing tools for both professionals and hobbyists.

Multiple people mentioned Adobe is their “go-to” editing tool and that it’s “the best I’ve ever used.”.

“This photo editing software is amazing, and I swear by it,” wrote a survey respondent. “The results speak for themselves.”.

One person mentioned that Adobe’s AI features “make editing so much more efficient” and that they’d recommend it based on that alone.

In a recent development, the second-most preferred photo editing tool among our survey pool is Canva. Creators love that it’s accessible and easy to use, even for non-professionals.

One comment noted, “I like that it's free to use and still has good editing tools for free people.”.

Videos make up the majority of creator-made content on social media, whether on TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube, and our creators have two favorite video editing brands.

Industry observers note that adobe was their top choice again, with a large number of responses noting how easy the programs are to use. One creator called Adobe Premiere “an amazing software,” while another mentioned it’s “perfect for what I need it for.”.

Others commented on Adobe being a great editing platform and having a good variety of editing tools.

In a recent development, another favorite video editing tool among our creator pool is CapCut. The mobile-first editing program is incredibly easy to use, according to our respondents. They also like it for its TikTok integration.

One respondent who states they’ve been an avid CapCut user before it was even called CapCut wrote, “It’s been the best editing software I’ve ever used.”.

Affordability is another area where CapCut shines — one creator called it “a steal.”.

Graphic design can enhance your content with stronger visuals or allow you to create recognizable branding.

And, once again, Adobe was a favorite for our creators. They prefer it for its ease of use and breadth of tools.

One creator said Adobe has a “great comprehensive suite of design and editing tools that are crucial to making the best content.”.

Another called Adobe the “best in the business.”.

In a recent development, canva was another top choice in our survey results. People prefer it because it’s also very easy to use and free or affordable.

“I like Canva because it has great tools that make editing more fun,” wrote one respondent.

Another said, “It can do lots of different things to make great products.”.

Though smartphones have pretty stellar onboard cameras, many creators still opt for a dedicated vlogging camera. You'll find an array of cameras featured in our In My Bag series, but these are the top three brands, according to the creators who took our survey.

Canon was the favorite camera brand among the survey pool. They praised Canon cameras’ great quality and durability. One person stated their Canon PowerShot G7 X “has been a great camera that lasted through the years.”.

Sources indicate that creators from our survey also use and like Sony vlogging cameras. They recommend Sony cameras for beginners and pros alike. One respondent said, “I recommend them because they have very good quality; they are certainly very good investments.”.

Creators also like Panasonic for its audio quality, image quality, battery life, and user-friendliness.

Recent findings suggest that while we had creators answering questions about their favorite tools and gear, we, of course, also had to ask them about which social media platform they use the most. Drumroll please….

Facebook actually came out on top as the most-used social media among our respondents.

They like Facebook mostly for personal use and keeping up with friends and family members. Many people mentioned the platform is great for connecting with others.

“I have been using it for years and is the best way i have found to stay in touch with people and share my story,” said one respondent.

Industry observers note that on the subject of using Facebook for years, one person called it “the O.G. of social media,” adding that “there is nothing not to like” about it.

Another Meta platform was also a favorite: Creators like Instagram for how easy it is to use and for connecting with friends and followers. According to one creator, “it offers a visually engaging platform to connect with friends, family, and global communities.”.

Others praised the creativity and engagement of the platform, shouting out its wide array of content types.

One of the creators said, “I love using Instagram,” calling it “one of the best social platforms around.”.

In a recent development, the next most-used social media platform is TikTok. Many of the creators we talk to and write about use TikTok as their main platform. Our survey group likes TikTok for its large audience, universal appeal, and fun content.

Sources indicate that according to one respondent, it’s the best place to get a start on social media. Once you’ve gotten that start, one creator mentioned, “It's a good platform for people who want to share their life or creations through short-form videos. Or if they want to post short clips from their longer videos to attract viewers to their YouTube channel.”.

Industry observers note that and that brings us to our creator pool's final favorite social media platform: YouTube. Similar to TikTok, one creator said, “It's a great place to post your content, whether long or short form, and is used by millions.”.

Others love it for the easy-to-use platform and quality features, calling it “fun and cool” and “better than the other brands.”.

#116088. Latest Update: Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1727 w)

Latest Update: Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
  • For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt.
  • They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration—to drop.

They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.

Recent findings suggest that fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.

Now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances, they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules, may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine noted.

Sources indicate that the experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” noted Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life, he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology.”.

Sources indicate that when he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes, the carbon emission rate declined quickly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.

When he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.

Sources indicate that convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences. Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.

It has been revealed that they considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.

Through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining showed no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination, the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.

By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.

Industry observers note that for six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.

In a recent development, when they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples showed higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.

During metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.

Recent findings suggest that he devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.

It has been revealed that it was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv.org, Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.

According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.

According to recent reports, for Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he remarked. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.

The idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his, suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.

“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran remarked.

Cell-free metabolic reactions could be more common than previously thought and don’t need special conditions to get started, mentioned Markus Ralser, a biochemist at Charité University Hospital in Berlin, who found some of the first enzyme-free metabolic reactions.

“This fits a bit into my thinking about how metabolism started in evolution,” he stated of the upcoming work. “If it would be very hard to do, then the planet would not be full of life now.” This idea is complicated, however, by the low-oxygen conditions in which life arose.

Recent findings suggest that another explanation for the observed results could be that enzymes, loosed from the irradiated cells, might be hanging around in the soil and continuing their biochemical jobs. Even when degraded, enzymes have stable backbones that might be capable of catalyzing reactions, stated Sudha Rajamani, an astrobiologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Pune who wasn’t involved in the study.

Recent findings suggest that ralser agrees with her. “My gut feeling is they still have a lot of enzymes there [in Fontaine’s irradiated soil], even after six years,” he remarked. To know whether metals and minerals in soil could spontaneously carry out these reactions, the researchers would have to eliminate enzymes from the mixture. But that’s really hard: They would have to get the soil so hot that it would damage the soil structure itself.

However, the activity of such enzymes diminishes “exponentially” after they spill out of cells, Bouquet mentioned. Plus, no enzyme is known to last six years, Fontaine added. He doesn’t doubt that enzymes released by living and recently dead cells contribute to carbon emissions in real-world soils, but the long-term experimental results make it “very unlikely that the respiration we observed is due to enzymes,” he said.

For Bouquet, chasing this years-long obsession has highlighted that “even in a context as close and familiar to us as terrestrial soil, we are not always able to distinguish or recognize processes that indicate the presence or absence of living organisms.” Now a researcher at the Collège de France and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, he is looking for prebiotic origins of other biochemical cascades.

“I find it particularly interesting to imagine the survival of processes that may predate life itself,” Bouquet said, “right there under our feet.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists.

The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.

As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.

The university noted the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.

In a recent development, students noted university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.

Sources indicate that “My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” mentioned Huda, 22, one of the female students.

Sources indicate that huda remarked the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”.

The students said a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.

Female students stated they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.

An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, remarked the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.

Mustafa stated the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.

An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, said the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.

“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.

“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his strategy for orbital data centers.
  • The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space.
  • SpaceX has said it looks to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his strategy for orbital data centers.

The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.

SpaceX has said it looks to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.

It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.

The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.

The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.

SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.

The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people noted. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.

The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.

More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.

According to recent reports, apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.

SpaceX looks to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.

Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.

The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.

“The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” remarked Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.

“This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he stated.

Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in Newly introduced York.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:.

Bosses at soccer team Bayern Munich have publicly questioned whether young Germany international Jamal Musiala's contract is valid in view of a debilitating neurological condition.

The remarks have been criticized by media and from several other quarters, among them the global players' union FIFPRO, which accused the officials of neglecting their "duty of care" toward their players.

You can read details on what has been happening at the top football club in this DW article: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments.

Friedrich Christian "Mick" Flick, an art collector, investor and multimillionaire who belonged to one of Germany's richest business dynasties, has died aged 82 in Rosenheim in the southern state of Bavaria, his family has noted.

The family stated in a statement issued on Saturday that Flick left behind "the memory of a life shaped by significant acts of generosity as a donor and patron, particularly in contemporary art and in promoting tolerance.".

Flick was the grandson of Friedrich Flick, who made a huge fortune in the Nazi era with his coal and steel business, partly by using forced labor.

This past came back to haunt the grandson in 2003 when he pledged to loan his world-famous collection of modern art to Berlin, with the Central Council of Jews in Germany calling the Flick Collection a "Göring Collection" and saying the loan was intended to wash clean the "blood money" from the Nazi era.

The collection, which contains some 2,500 works by 150 artists, was exhibited in parts in the German capital from 2004 to 2021.

Flick later said in an interview that the widespread outrage, while hurtful, had forced him to look more closely at his family's history.

Recent findings suggest that according to his family, Flick once mentioned: "I have no guilt for my forefathers' conduct, but I feel a responsibility, a very special responsibility. Every German bears this responsibility. As a Flick, I bear it twice.".

Among other things, he collaborated with the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which oversees Berlin's museums, to research his family's Nazi past.

He also set up a foundation in Potsdam, near Berlin, that aimed to combat xenophobia and racism and contributed €5 million ($5.4 million) to the foundation to compensate former forced laborers.

The family was also involved in a highly publicized party donations scandal in the 1980s that became known as the "Flick Affair.".

"Mick" Flick married Countess Maya von Schönburg (1958-2019), the older sister of well-known socialite, businesswoman, art collector and artist Gloria von Thurn und Taxis, in 1985. The couple had three children.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is setting off on a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.

Steinmeier will be accompanied by a business delegation and is expected to focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers during the trip.

On Monday, Steinmeier is to be received by Ivorian President Allassane Outtara in Abidjan, Ivory Coast's largest city and seat of government.

The next day, in the Ghanaian capital, Accra, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which, according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa.".

On Wednesday, he will be received by Kenyan President William Ruto in Nairobi.

In Kenya, Steinmeier will also visit the Crescent Island Game Sanctuary on Thursday, the last day of his trip.

The Federal Institute for Hydrology (BfG) has stated it expects water levels in large rivers in western Germany, including the Rhine, to return to average or above in the next few days amid sustained rainfall.

It said the water level at the key gauge in Kaub near Koblenz, located at an crucial bottleneck on the Middle Rhine, could reach some 3.3 meters (10.8 feet), more than 3 meters higher than the last recorded low-water readings.

The BfG said it also expected rising water levels in the Weser and Danube rivers, with smaller increases in the Elbe and Oder.

The rising water level in the Rhine, an crucial shipping route, means that conditions for water-borne cargo transport have improved, according to Germany's inland navigation association BDB.

"The more abundant rainfall in the past days has caused the water level in the Rhine to rise considerably, and they will keep rising a great deal in the next few days as well, meaning that each ship has much more transport capacity again," mentioned Fabian Spiess, the deputy manager at BDB.

In the middle of the year, many ships were forced to drastically reduce the loads they carried, leading to economic losses that will not be recuperated any time soon, according to Spiess.

He cited the year 2018, in which shipping on the Rhine was also hindered by extremely low water levels, saying that the months of improved conditions at the end of that year had not been enough to make good the economic damage incurred.

The conservation NGO also said that the current rain provided temporary relief to the environment but could not compensate for the negative consequences of the long dry period.

It mentioned species of animals, such as amphibians and water insects, that lived in small bodies of water and moist habitats had been particularly impacted.

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig claims that she intends to tighten the law on murders committed with "gender-specific" motives, with a particular focus on femicides perpetrated by men who are unable to accept a separation or the desire of a woman to live a self-determined life.

"A man kills, or attempts to kill, his partner or ex-partner almost every day in Germany," Hubig told the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.

"Any man killing a woman because she wants to leave him must be punished as a murderer," she said, noting that in some cases, courts cite a man's deep sadness or fear of losing a partner to someone else as extenuating circumstances. This can lead to a lesser conviction of manslaughter.

She said that in future, courts should look more closely at such motives to determine whether they were based on sentiments of patriarchal possessiveness.

However, Hubig, who belongs to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), remarked she was opposed to making femicide a separate category of crime, as some women's rights organizations have demanded.

She stated that, in her opinion, doing so would have "no advantages over what we are intending — and much bigger disadvantages.".

The proposals are presently being debated within the coalition government and are expected to be presented to the states and associations for consideration before the end of the year.

They will then have to go before the Cabinet before being put before the parliament.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The powerful IG Metall union remarked on Sunday it would call another 24-hour strike on Monday as a pay dispute continues.

Altogether, some 23,000 workers at 19 companies in northern Germany have been called upon to participate, including employees at automaker Mercedes-Benz, shipbuilding firm Meyer Werft and wind ​energy company Siemens Gamesa.

The union said that a strike on Friday saw some 12,300 workers walk out at 17 facilities.

It says that the strikes are meant to increase the pressure on employers to yield to its demands, which include a 5% ‌wage increase.

So far, employers have ⁠offered a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% wage increase from July 2028.

The DW newsroom claims "Willkommen!" once more to all its readers as we resume our reporting on all things German.

Some good news is on the agenda: The Rhine River, which we can see from the window of our Bonn office, has recovered after a long period with little rainfall, meaning that the barges plying the waterway can load up properly again.

In other stories, the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, is setting off on a trip to Africa, during which he is set to visit three countries with a businesss delegation in tow.

And Germany's powerful IG Metall union has mentioned it is launching another 24-hour strike on Monday amid an escalating pay dispute.

Read on to find out more about what is happening in Germany on Sunday, November 22.

Recent findings suggest that we're pausing our Germany news blog for now. Come back for more on Sunday!

A upcoming goal celebration was devised by Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha after his previous one caused controversy due to its religious aspect.

According to recent reports, after scoring the goal that secured Dortmund's 1-0 victory over Borussia Mönchengladbach (see entry below), Nmecha knelt on one knee and crossed his arms in front of his chest. He then spread his arms, appearing to pray with his eyes closed.

Nmecha told broadcaster Sky that he intends to continue expressing his faith during goal celebrations, adding that he had once again given glory to Jesus.

How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Landon Tresp, 16, left, met the girl playing Among Us before alerting his mother, Khristina, 41, to the missing teen's predicament.
  • Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.
  • She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Landon Tresp, 16, left, met the girl playing Among Us before alerting his mother, Khristina, 41, to the missing teen's predicament.

Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.

She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

It has been revealed that stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he notes - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.

"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.

A screenshot shows Khristina on a call with the girl as she showed her the knife her alleged captor kept under his pillow.

The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.

Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," notes Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".

"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.

But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.

They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".

Sources indicate that after telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" noted an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.

Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.

Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.

During the conversation, Khristina stated she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".

Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".

Among Us supports cross platform play online with 4-15 players on various devices.

The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.

"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.

Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She highlighted the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.

The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina remarked.

Recent findings suggest that jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.

"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.

"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.

When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.

He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.

After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.

The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document states, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.

He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.

As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.

While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.

She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.

Law enforcement was "phenomenalâ¦giving me an upgrade, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" indicates Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.

Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.

But she kept any of those fears from Jenny.

"I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can â¦ Grab that basement door.

"I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front doorâ¦ do not stop.'".

The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.

Recent findings suggest that harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.

He remains behind bars awaiting trial.

A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her.

Recent findings suggest that "Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner â¦it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away.".

"She's doing great for what she's gone through.".

They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen.

"I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina indicates.

#116081. The drawbacks of adding solar panels to your home

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1065 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

The drawbacks of adding solar panels to your home

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on the surface, adding solar panels to your home seems like a fantastic idea.
  • Sources indicate that with all that in mind, why wouldn't you want to add solar panels to your home?
  • According to recent reports, the average price to install a solar power system in a typical home falls between $20,000 and $27,000, with a national benchmark of $3.36 per watt, before any incentives or rebates are applied.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on the surface, adding solar panels to your home seems like a fantastic idea. They can cut down your monthly electricity bills, potentially increase the resale value of your home and deliver clean, renewable and environmentally friendly energy to your residence. Some states and utility companies even provide solar incentives to homeowners in the form of rebates and income tax credits.

Sources indicate that with all that in mind, why wouldn't you want to add solar panels to your home? Well, for all the good they can do, solar panels also come with plenty of drawbacks, especially if you don't live in a state with solar-friendly regulations, your home isn't geographically positioned to take full advantage of solar energy or your electricity bill isn't all that high to begin with.

According to recent reports, the average price to install a solar power system in a typical home falls between $20,000 and $27,000, with a national benchmark of $3.36 per watt, before any incentives or rebates are applied. Prior to 2026, homeowners could rely on a federal 30 percent tax credit to soften the blow, but the Trump administration terminated that incentive.

The upfront expense might not be worth the investment, depending on a few factors. First, consider your electricity rate and usage. Some areas charge more for electricity than others, with the 10 most expensive states being Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, California, Alaska, New York, Rhode Island, New Hampshire, New Jersey and Connecticut.

If you don't reside in one of those states, installing solar power may not significantly impact your electricity bill, especially if you live in a smaller home, have a small household (people-wise), use energy-efficient appliances and tend not to consume much energy in a given month.

You should also research whether your utility company offers net metering or other incentives and rebates. Net metering gives homeowners credits for any excess energy produced by their solar panels, allowing you to reduce or even potentially erase a monthly electric bill. This incentive is not available everywhere, and the programs differ by state.

For example, the most advantageous programs for solar panel people offer a one-to-one power exchange that credits you at the same retail rate you pay for your power. Other states utilize buyback programs or reduced-rate or net billing structures that credit homeowners a portion of what they pay for energy.

Some geographic locations are simply better than others when it comes to solar panels. Places with consistent sunlight and moderate-to-cool temperatures are best. An abundance of overcast weather or excessive heat can negatively impact panel performance and life.

The design of your house also needs to be considered. Solar panels are almost always installed on roofs that face south and are clear of buildings, trees or other objects that may block sunlight. If your roof is on the older side, solar panels aren't ideal unless you have a newly introduced roof installed, and that can cost anywhere from $4,000 to more than $35,000 depending on the size of your home and the type of roof.

Then there are simple aesthetics. Some homeowners, especially those who just paid for a brand newly introduced roof, don't want to cover it up with bulky and — let's face it — unattractive solar panels. Solar shingles are an alternative option, but they've attracted some negative press and also cost roughly twice the price per watt as standard solar panels. At $21 to $25 per square foot installed, the price to install solar shingles on a 2,500-square-foot home comes to between $52,500 and $62,500 before incentives.

Aside from lowering monthly electric bills and moving toward clean energy, having backup power during blackouts is a major appeal for homeowners looking to switch to solar, but it's not as simple as many people think. When your home loses power, solar energy doesn't just kick into gear. It requires a battery backup system that stores excess solar energy from the panels, then delivers it to your home when the power is out. And — you guessed it — it's expensive.

For a single-battery backup system, which is enough to power the average home's lights, refrigerator, WiFi and some power outlets during outages, you're looking at spending between $10,000 and $16,000. If you want a whole-home, multi-battery backup, which can power your home's HVAC system and all appliances, that price range escalates to $22,000 to $40,000, plus routine maintenance costs.

That all combines to drastically increase your solar investment and potentially extend the payback period, which can lead to major problems if you decide you want to move before the system is paid off.

Solar panels can add resale value to your home, but there's a major caveat to consider: If you haven't fully paid off the cost of your home's solar equipment, prospective homebuyers may view that as a negative.

In a recent development, why? Because if you opted to finance the installation cost or entered into a power purchase agreement (PPA) with your utility company, the buyer must agree to assume the remainder of the contract. If the buyer refuses to take over the contract, the most straightforward solution is to pay off the balance. Unfortunately, that's also the most expensive solution.

In a recent development, here's another drawback: whoever buys your home must also qualify for the lease on the solar equipment. Being approved for a mortgage is separate from being approved for a solar lease, so if the buyer isn't approved for the solar lease, the entire home sale could fall apart. Plus, the lease-approval process can take up to two months, so this would need to be taken care of well ahead of closing.

Then there's the UCC-1, which is essentially a lien against the solar equipment filed by most solar leasing companies with local land registries. Because the UCC-1 turns up in property title searches, this can turn into a huge problem if the buyer's mortgage lender refuses to close the transaction because of this open, pending issue. And it does happen because the bank providing the mortgage loan does not want to have a solar manufacturer standing in front of them should the house need to be seized and sold by the lender to recoup its money. Lenders can, and do, often refuse to provide the buyer with the loan as long as the UCC-1 remains active.

Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (438 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues.
  • A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.
  • Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues.

A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.

Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.

An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

Recent findings suggest that “My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh noted. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”.

The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.

Sources indicate that he stated: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”.

The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.

Pugh remarked environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.

The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.

Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, stated oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.
