General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

NASA’s upcoming Moon plan is taking shape, but some major questions remain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.
  • Sources indicate that for SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships.
  • In a recent development, early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

Sources indicate that for SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

In a recent development, early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

It has been revealed that the Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.

Other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.

According to recent reports, ars recently spoke with Steve Creech, the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.

Sources indicate that for Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a Newly introduced Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.

According to recent reports, then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.

It has been revealed that NASA changed the plan for the Artemis III mission earlier this year, rerouting the flight plan from a lunar mission to a low-Earth orbit mission. This means the Artemis program’s first crewed lunar landing will be on Artemis IV, targeted to launch before the end of 2028.

So, why is Artemis III seemingly testing so much more with Blue Origin than with Starship? Creech told Ars that a big reason is to maintain SpaceX’s focus on orbital refueling. Blue Origin no longer requires in-space refueling for Artemis landing missions. Also, SpaceX has extensive experience with life support systems with its Dragon crewed spacecraft. Blue Origin has comparatively little.

Sources indicate that “The bigger challenges for [SpaceX] were the prop transfer and getting to the uncrewed landing demo,” Creech noted. “The thing that we’re going to learn more with Starship is, when we dock with Orion, they will have control of the attitude, control of the stack. That integrated stack control will be on the Starship side. So, with that huge of a vehicle, I think we’re going to learn more on that.

It has been revealed that “With Blue, we’re going to have Orion control the stack for this mission,” Creech said. “When we get to a later mission, the Blue lander with fully loaded prop will have to control the stack. But with Blue, trying to mitigate risk, we’re going to have Orion do that.”.

Sources indicate that artemis III will be Blue Origin’s first time flying a crew cabin for orbital spaceflight. Blue Origin has experience with suborbital space tourism, but those flights were brief and didn’t require the level of advanced life support necessary for longer durations. Blue Origin and NASA will emphasize those test objectives on Artemis III.

“I think SpaceX’s part was really, we need to focus on the docking,” Creech stated. “If we added a crew cabin, that would slow us down on the other things and not add to what we’re already doing.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Starship on Artemis III will have a full complement of Raptor engines and a docking port on its nose. Blue Moon will not have any main engines when it links up with Orion on Artemis III, only a set of smaller thrusters for pointing control and minor maneuvers.

Recent findings suggest that “With Blue, you don’t have a BE-7 engine, you don’t have the cryo tanks,” Creech remarked. “They’re representing the mass of the lander when it comes back from the surface because we think that’s the most critical case. But it does have the crew cabin.”.

While there’s no Starship life support demonstration on Artemis III, NASA added a new milestone to SpaceX’s Moon lander contract to test parts of its crew cabin on the ground. The additional testing involves construction of a prototype crew compartment, called Cabin One, at SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, Texas.

Sources indicate that NASA levied fresh test requirements on Blue Origin, too. The company plans to launch its first Blue Moon test mission early next year after a monthslong delay caused by a rocket explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in May. This version of Blue Moon, known as Mark 1, has a single hydrogen-fueled BE-7 main engine. Future human-rated landers from Blue Origin will have three.

“One of the things we added into the program in the last year is, we really felt like we needed a test of the three-engine configuration,” Creech remarked. The hotfire test of the three-engine Blue Moon propulsion unit will occur inside a vacuum chamber at NASA’s In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio.

According to recent reports, this year’s Artemis shakeup did more than change the flight plan for Artemis III. Engineers also altered the architecture for subsequent lunar landing missions. The updated looks will make life easier for teams working on Starship and Blue Moon. That’s not necessarily the case for Orion.

Recent findings suggest that “Our previous architecture for both these landers required a 90-day loiter in lunar orbit for Orion to arrive,” Creech stated. “That was something that, for both of these landers, drove a lot of complexity, and a lot of it made the lander job really hard.”.

The fresh concept of operations removes some of that complexity, according to NASA.

“One of the things we changed was that 90-day loiter,” Creech noted. “SpaceX, they solved it by saying let’s do an Earth orbit rendezvous with Orion, and take Orion to the Moon. For both Blue Origin and SpaceX, we have updated their requirements to a four-day surface day initially. Before, our initial missions were six-and-a-half days.”.

Industry observers note that the six-and-a-half-day surface stay was baked into the Artemis architecture because the Orion spacecraft was originally planned to settle into a long, looping path around the Moon, called a near-rectilinear halo orbit. This orbit was predicated by the expected location of NASA’s now-canceled Gateway lunar space station. That, in turn, was driven by Orion’s inability to reach an orbit closer to the Moon.

In a recent development, now, instead of rendezvousing with Starship near the Moon on landing missions, Orion will link up with Starship in high-Earth orbit. From there, Starship will propel it toward the Moon.

In a recent development, what’s still unclear, however, is whether SpaceX will have to refuel Starship at an altitude above low-Earth orbit. A graphic presented by Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, last month illustrated this possibility with a “final tanking orbit” before Starship docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re still working that out,” Creech said. “We’re making progress, but where we actually rendezvous with Orion is still in trade, so that’s why you saw a little bit of fuzziness there.”.

For missions using Blue Moon, the lander will connect with Orion in orbit around the Moon. Blue Origin’s updated plans do away with the requirement for in-space refueling but will still require four rolls out of the company’s Upcoming Glenn rocket, one for the Blue Moon lander itself and three with transfer stages to boost it out of Earth orbit to the Moon.

A upcoming stretched Centaur upper stage for the Space Launch System should give the rocket energy to send Orion to low-lunar orbit, which it could not reach with the current version of SLS. NASA has not determined if the new Centaur exploration stage will be ready in time for Artemis IV. If not, Artemis IV could fly with the last of NASA’s in-stock SLS upper stages.

NASA is also waiting to decide which lander to use on Artemis IV. In either case, two of Orion’s four astronauts will transfer into the landers for the final descent to the lunar surface for a four-day stay, then take off and return to Orion.

Sources indicate that starship and Blue Moon must each complete an uncrewed landing demonstration before a crewed lunar mission. The landing demos are targeted for late 2027 or early 2028, Creech remarked, but they won’t necessarily test everything crews will need when they head for the lunar south pole.

In a recent development, starship’s elevator, for example, is not part of SpaceX’s uncrewed landing demonstration. Engineers will use a test lab at Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama to check the elevator’s performance in a simulated lunar environment.

NASA did not initially require SpaceX or Blue Origin to prove their landers could take off from the Moon before a crew mission. Government officials later added the lunar takeoff requirement for each tech giant’s uncrewed landing demos.

For now, NASA is leaving the details of the uncrewed takeoff demo up to SpaceX and Blue Origin. During Apollo, NASA’s lunar lander never landed on the Moon before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin descended to the Sea of Tranquility. NASA did, however, fly a dress rehearsal around the Moon on Apollo 10 that included a test of the lunar module’s landing abort capability.

“Where we are today is, Blue will land and then do a full ascent back to the rendezvous point with Orion,” Creech stated. “With SpaceX. They will land, they will take off again, get to main stage on the engines, and then they will do another landing on the surface.”.

That could change. Today’s strategy gives SpaceX two shots at proving Starship can safely land on the Moon, but it comes with trade-offs.

“When I came into the program, I was like, ‘Why are we not going all the way to the rendezvous point?’” said Creech, who took over as HLS program manager in 2025. “Some of my key people felt strongly we would get more out of the way we’re doing it now. There are others that have different opinions… We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”.

For Starship, orbital refueling remains the key to the Moon. SpaceX’s propellant transfer demonstration will involve two Starships, one introduced from Florida and another from Texas, docking together in low-Earth orbit and transferring a “meaningful” amount of propellant from one ship to the other, Creech noted.

Sources indicate that “The first quarter of next year, we will see a long-awaited propellant transfer test from SpaceX, where they launch two Starships in pretty close proximity, actually dock, and transfer, we’re calling it a meaningful amount, of propellant,” Creech told Ars. “That is going to be a big learning point if they pull that off, because their architecture depends on propellant aggregation and multiple propellant flights.”.

Sources indicate that the propellant transfer test will mark the first time one spacecraft has offloaded a significant quantity of cryogenic propellants—in this case, methane and liquid oxygen—onto another vehicle in space. It is the culmination of decades of government and commercial research on cryogenic orbital refueling. The results will tell engineers how much of the propellant will be lost from boil-off during the transfer.

Sources indicate that that is one reason why there’s still so much ambiguity about how many Starship refueling tankers SpaceX will need to launch to give the Starship lunar lander enough gas to fly to the Moon. Without refueling, Starships are restricted to flights in low-Earth orbit.

The low end of the estimate for Starship tankers is six to eight refueling flights to support a Starship lunar mission. Those numbers come from Elon Musk, SpaceX’s founder and CEO, and fall below NASA’s own conservative planning figure of 20 refueling debuts. Musk’s figures hinge on future Starship upgrades to reach the vehicle’s full potential. SpaceX’s goal is to get Starship’s lift capacity up to 100 to 200 metric tons of payload to low-Earth orbit. Today’s version of Starship, known as Starship V3, is still far short of 100 metric tons of payload capacity.

For context, a Starship carries 1,600 metric tons of propellant with its tanks full. Refueling flights using future, fully optimized Starships might be able to fill those tanks with as few as six tankers. That is not the case today.

According to recent reports, spaceX is working on a taller, heavier Starship called Starship V4. It will fly with nine Raptor engines, an upgrade over the six-engine variant flying today. In 2025, Musk noted Starship V4’s first launch was targeted for 2027. There hasn’t been a recent patch to the schedule for Starship V4.

The initial Artemis lunar missions will use Starship V3, Creech said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This tool allows you to search for exactly the type of content you want to see.
  • According to recent reports, youTube is a core hub of entertainment for millions of people.
  • As of October 2026, the platform introduced custom feeds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This tool allows you to search for exactly the type of content you want to see.

According to recent reports, youTube is a core hub of entertainment for millions of people. More than 20 million videos hit the platform every day, according to data from YouTube. That's a lot of content to sort through when you're trying to find something to watch. If you're a regular watcher of YouTube, your homepage is probably already leaning into your interests, be they comedy specials, home improvement tutorials or music videos from the '90s. But if you're looking to exert some more control and specificity over what the algorithm suggests to you, YouTube has a way to do it by offloading your playlist curation to AI.

As of October 2026, the platform introduced custom feeds. In short, custom feeds let you use natural language to set up feeds around the kind of content you want to see more of and keep it in a spot that's easy to access. Here's how to set up those feeds if you want to fine-tune your homepage.

If you want to tailor what you're seeing on YouTube more to your tastes, you can start by building a custom feed using prompts. At the top of your homepage, tap the + sign (you may also see the words "Custom feed"). From there, you can type into the box whatever you are interested in seeing. For example, YouTube gives examples like "I want retro tech nostalgia: 80s commercials, vintage PCs, CRT glow." Another example demonstrates that you don't even have to get that specific. You could ask for a feed along the lines of, "I want to explore something completely different beyond my usual feed.".

Once you create a feed, you'll find it at the top of the screen so you can access it when you want. YouTube noted that you can always use the prompt box at the top of a feed if you want to tweak what you're seeing.

Industry observers note that if you like the idea of custom feeds, you can save up to three without a YouTube Premium account. If you do happen to have a YouTube Premium account, you can save up to eight. Regardless of your subscription, as long as you are signed into your account, the custom feeds you created will sync across mobile and desktop. It's also crucial to remember that custom feeds will expire if you don't use them for 30 days. If this happens, though, you can always create a newly introduced prompt. YouTube also pointed out that the feeds are subject to the platform's community guidelines.

So far, custom feeds are only available in English in the United States. You also need to have search history enabled to use the feature.

The rollout of custom feeds wasn't the only change YouTube brought to the homepage. Specifically on the mobile app, you might have noticed a row of feeds across the top of the page with categories like Live or Music. Some of these feeds might depend on your subscription. For example, you won't see the Movies & TV feed if you don't have any Primetime Channel subscriptions. Additionally, YouTube mentioned that the Subs feed, as in your subscriptions, moved to the top bar. If you want to exit your feeds, you can always tap on the Home tab on the left and go back to what you'd normally see on your homepage.

In its blogpost, YouTube noted these changes are part of a series of updates to shape "a more seamless Home experience." So, if you're looking to create some feeds based on more specific interests that you can easily get to from the homepage, YouTube's custom feeds feature might be worth a prompt.

Breaking: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source remarked, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source remarked, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical upcoming insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it notes is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

Recent findings suggest that CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

In a recent development, the balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, mentioned at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

According to recent reports, the surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jay Clayton was pressed on Trump’s characterization of Putin during media appearances on Sunday.

Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.

Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”.

On CNN’s State of the Union, Dana Bash asked Clayton whether he also thinks Putin is a friend to the US.

“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen,” said Clayton on Sunday. “Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable and, in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”.

Bash pressed on whether Clayton personally agrees that Putin should be considered a friend.

“Dana, in different contexts, you can use different words. The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable,” Clayton replied.

Speaking with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on This Week, Clayton made similar comments, saying that “using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate” in the context of the summit.

According to recent reports, “That conversation, that picture – historic, historic picture – was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton remarked on Sunday, referring to Trump’s post. “In that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate.”.

Clayton also dodged when asked again whether he thinks Putin should be considered a friend to the United States.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton responded.

Last week, Trump sidestepped questions about his views on a friendship with Putin.

Recent findings suggest that “I can’t speak to America,” Trump said in a press briefing. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing.”.

Trump’s characterization of Putin has sparked backlash from US lawmakers and officials abroad.

“Who is he? He’s the man who has abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine, detained Americans wrongfully, and continues to do so daily,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media.

“Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer added. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.”.

“It’s beyond me,” Senator Jeanne Shaheen noted in an interview with MS NOW. “I don’t understand the president’s admiration and cozying up to Vladimir Putin, who is a war criminal.”.

Trump’s comments also drew rebukes abroad, including from the deputy leader of the rightwing party Reform UK.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake,” Richard Tice told Sky News. “He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have remarked, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”.

Trump’s description of ​Putin as a friend also drew criticism from European ​allies of Ukraine. “Mr ‌Putin is ​not our ​friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk remarked.

Separately, Clayton also faced questions about the recent spate of technology outages across the US and noted Americans should expect more disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems.

“And ​as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, ⁠interruptions in service,” Clayton said on CNN’s State of the Union program. “That is ⁠going to happen.”.

Associated Press contributed reporting.

#116034. Industry News: China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1139 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was supposed to be a breakthrough year.
  • Much more than diplomatic wording is at stake.
  • A code of conduct is to set up rules for parties dealing with one another and prevent incidents at sea from escalating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was supposed to be a breakthrough year. The Philippines had intended to set up a code of conduct with China for the South China Sea during its 2026 ASEAN presidency. However, at the summit in Manila in mid-November they had to abandon their goal. Some 80% of the text had been negotiated, declared Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, but the key areas of dispute had remained unsolved.

Much more than diplomatic wording is at stake. The South China Sea is one of the world's most vital shipping routes, it is rich in fishing grounds and may harbor significant oil and gas reserves. Primarily, however, it's a region of strategic competition: With its so-called Nine-Dash Line (often drawn in red), China claims a large portion of the sea. Its claims overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.

A code of conduct is to set up rules for parties dealing with one another and prevent incidents at sea from escalating. However, opinions differ, particularly with regard to its binding nature and its geographic scope.

Recent findings suggest that "The basic problem with establishing such a code of conduct is that China is supremely powerful and has no real interest in a legally binding agreement," remarked political scientist Andreas Ufen, Southeast Asia expert at the German Institute of Global and Area Studies (GIGA). Beijing had little incentive to impose restrictions on itself as long as it was able to pursue its interests in the region even without such an agreement, Ufen told DW.

In a recent development, the Paracel Islands serve as an example of just how difficult the unresolved challenges are. In China, the group of islands is known as Xisha, in Vietnam as Hoang-Sa. Hanoi apparently wants to include them in the code's geographic scope, but China rejects this. An agreement within the ASEAN framework could indirectly affect the territorial claims of the parties involved.

It has been revealed that "A fundamental problem is that so far there's no consensus on whether the code of conduct should be legally binding," said Felix Heiduk, head of research division Asia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). China and the ASEAN nations have been negotiating an agreement for 12 years without major progress so far.

In a recent development, there were reservations about such a treaty not only in China but also in other ASEAN countries. They would subsequently have to ratify a legally binding agreement under international law in their own countries. A non-binding code of conduct, by contrast, would be little more than a voluntary declaration of intent, Ufen told DW.

It has been revealed that the definition of an "incident" is controversial as well. Are coast guard missions with use of water cannons included? Or blockades of supply vessels? Or is the code only applicable when military force is involved? This will determine which actions will be covered by the regulations in the future.

"These are by no means just technical details. Their clarification determines to a great extent whether the code of conduct will in fact be effective or will ultimately remain only a non-binding declaration of intent," Heiduk stated. An agreement without valid commitments would bring about little change.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that ufen views China's attitude as a strategic calculation. "I believe that China is interested in keeping the conflict simmering, so to speak, without having to commit itself to a truly binding legal regulation," he stated. In this way, Beijing could strengthen its position in the South China Sea without limiting its room for maneuver.

According to recent reports, at the same time there are also diverging interests within the ASEAN group. The 11 member states are by no means united. The Philippines and Vietnam are particularly vocal in their opposition to China. Malaysia and Indonesia pursue a more restrained approach. Cambodia and Laos have close economic ties with Beijing and don't have any territorial claims in the South China Sea.

Sources indicate that "From the start of the negotiations, the lack of unity within ASEAN has been a problem. In a way, it's a permanent obstacle," Heiduk said. The group makes decisions based on the consensus principle, which basically means that every member state can block a unified position. Recurring confrontations between China and the Philippines exacerbated the problem by undermining trust and making it more difficult to reach compromises.

Ufen also believes that diverging interests are a key impediment. "Reconciling them is extremely difficult," he noted. China could take advantage of the discord. Beijing preferred bilateral negotiations with individual countries rather than dealing with an entire, united group of nations.

A study published by the Singapore-based Yusof Ishak Institute (ISEAS)reaches similar conclusions. Not only China but internal divisions within ASEAN stalled negotiations. The authors warn against exclusively relying on a comprehensive, legally binding treaty. Initially, partial agreements  — for example, on crisis communication, rescue operations at sea or maritime environment protection — could be a first step. Developing the 2002 agreement on a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea could also be an intermediate step.

According to recent reports, ufen doubts whether Beijing is interested in a binding result. "For this reason, I can't really imagine that China has a real interest in a code of conduct that includes legally binding regulations," he stated.

It has been revealed that heiduk warns against overestimating the significance of a potential agreement. "Even if the code of conduct was signed at some point, in whichever shape, that would in no way solve the conflict in the South China Sea," he noted. The code could regulate how to handle incidents, but it could not eliminate territorial disputes and competing claims to maritime areas.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This constitutes the dilemma for ASEAN nations as well, whose foreign policy oscillates between China and US ties: An agreement that's as binding as possible could fail because China and individual member states have reservations. A weak, non-binding code, however, could give the impression everyone agreed but would hardly change conduct at sea.

The American Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) summed up the situationafter the summit in Manila: "Whatever progress was made this year, it is almost certain that the hardest sticking points remain unresolved.".

Negotiations will be continued in 2027 under Singapore's chairmanship. Whether this will turn into more than just another diplomatic effort will depend on whether China is prepared to submit itself to regulations which limit its scope of action and whether ASEAN will be able to reach a consensus.

This article was originally published in German.

The advantages of using a USB-C docking station

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plus, there are differences between a USB-C hub and a docking station.
  • In a recent development, laptops have been getting thinner and lighter from year to year, and they have become so powerful that many people choose a laptop as their main computer.
  • A USB-C docking station is a box that connects to your laptop through a single USB-C cable and gives it a full set of ports.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus, there are differences between a USB-C hub and a docking station.

In a recent development, laptops have been getting thinner and lighter from year to year, and they have become so powerful that many people choose a laptop as their main computer. But a thin body means fewer ports, and a desktop setup with a screen, mouse, webcam and keyboard requires a lot of them. If you have a laptop and still want the full desktop experience, a USB-C docking station can be the solution you're looking for.

A USB-C docking station is a box that connects to your laptop through a single USB-C cable and gives it a full set of ports. USB-C docking stations reduce cord clutter, add more ports to your setup and can keep your laptop's own ports from wearing down.

Sources indicate that the biggest advantage of a dock is simplicity. One single cable connects the laptop to its peripherals. That means you can come home and plug in all your devices with one plug; you can also grab your laptop on your way out just as swiftly. Monitors, a keyboard, a webcam and a charger no longer need to be reconnected every time the laptop comes and goes, and your desk stays tidier because the cables run to the dock instead of the laptop.

A dock can also add ports your laptop doesn't have. Depending on the model, you can get HDMI or DisplayPort outputs for external monitors, more USB ports, an SD card reader and an Ethernet port for a stable wired internet connection. A thin laptop that comes with three or four ports can end up with a dozen.

The third advantage is less wear on your laptop. Plugging and unplugging several cables over and over puts strain on the ports, and a dock takes that job over. Instead of plugging several cables into the laptop every day, you plug in just one.

According to recent reports, if you only need a few basic connections, a USB-C hub is the cheaper option. Hubs have roughly four to 10 ports and cost anywhere between $30 and $150. Docking stations generally have more ports, come with their own DC power adapter, and cost more, with some higher-end models costing more than $400. A dock can give you a full desktop setup with multiple monitors, plus more ports of every kind, and the higher-end Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 models can run multiple displays, Ethernet, audio and laptop charging through that one cable. If that sounds like what you need, here are the best docking stations for laptops.

Industry observers note that before buying, it's worth checking a few things, because not every dock works with every laptop. A USB-C port only outputs video if it supports DisplayPort Alt Mode or is a Thunderbolt or USB4 port, and the dock needs to support Power Delivery pass-through at your laptop's required wattage. If you initiative to work with the lid closed, keep the power plugged in, since the laptop draws more power with an external monitor attached.

Get those details right and a dock quietly does its job, providing a laptop that goes back to being portable by unplugging just one cable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years.
  • Upcoming York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new blueprint from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
  • Mamdani on Friday unveiled a proposal to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four upcoming jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years.

Upcoming York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new blueprint from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

Mamdani on Friday unveiled a proposal to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four upcoming jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Looks to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

In a recent development, it houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the Newly introduced York City correction officers' union.

"[B]uilding a fresh system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges.".

"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in Upcoming York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she noted.

Industry observers note that the jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.

Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.

In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani remarked Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.

Latest York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the proposal.

Mamdani's office stated the city would open up four upcoming jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

Recent findings suggest that the mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.

Mamdani remarked his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across Newly introduced York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.

He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health challenges.

Kaplan remarked Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.

The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (Â£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

  • Whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land.
  • The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.
  • Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.

The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.

Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.

There’s a ton to like about this 100-watt universal travel adapter from reliable travel brand Ceptics. It covers more than 200 countries and can charge multiple gadgets in a hurry. The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom. But what makes this travel adapter my favorite is the retractable USB-C cable. It’s around 25 inches long, the end sticks to the adapter magnetically, and it saves you from having to pack an extra cord. The cable can deliver up to 100 watts in total. The USB-C ports support up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports go up to 12 watts.

It has been revealed that for all of its strengths, though, it does provide an unfortunate lack of any grounding. Grounding is meant to reduce the risk of an electric shock if there’s a fault, such as a loose wire inside a device with a metal case. (This video explains grounding well.) Thankfully, there’s overload protection with a 10-amp fuse, and it also comes with a spare. But you should not use this adapter with any device with a third metal ground pin on its plug.

I also tested the 140-watt Ceptics 6-in-1 model ($51), which omits the cable but has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, and the excellent 70-watt model ($40), which has the retractable cable but fewer ports and loses the extra outlet. Both are great alternatives.

Perhaps the smallest travel adapter that's still practical to use, the Epicka Air measures 3.46 x 1.97 inches and is just 1.19 inches thick, with the prongs folded away. It’s easy to pack but still feels reasonably sturdy in use. You get one USB-A and three USB-C ports. The first three ports offer up to 15 watts apiece, and the last USB-C port on the right can go up to 65 watts. But 65 watts is also the maximum output across the four ports, so it gets divided if you plug in multiple devices. But if you use the AC outlet too, and you can charge up to five devices at once.

In a recent development, when I first tested the 40-watt version ($25), I wasn’t sure about this travel adapter, but after using the 65-watt model for a while, I’ve grown to like it. I still think this style of folding design can be a bit fiddly to use, and the prongs sometimes fold back if you bump them while plugging in. But the placement of the EU prongs in the middle helps it stay plugged in more reliably than some larger sliding cube adapters; the US prongs lock into place, and I didn’t have any concerns with the UK prongs.

Industry observers note that this budget Ceptics device proves that you don’t need to spend that much money to snag one of the best travel adapters. It covers more than 150 countries, with sliders you push to reveal the three most common international plugs—EU, UK, and US. You can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia or China. The sliders lock into place securely, and there’s a button on the side for retracting them. This plug’s universal outlet can recharge your power-hungry devices, like laptops and camera batteries. Two USB-C and two USB-A ports on the bottom, plus a USB-C port on the side, can handle phones, tablets, smartwatches, and Kindles. Each USB-C port can deliver up to 15 watts, and each USB-A port up to 12 watts. While it's not as fast as some of my picks above, you won't care if you tend to charge your gadgets overnight.

Industry observers note that there’s no grounding, so don’t plug devices with a third metal ground pin into this adapter. There is an 8-amp fuse for safety, and it comes with a spare. It is also certified by RoHS and CE.

Industry observers note that what I love about this sturdy, compact plug adapter is the lack of sliding pins or moving parts to worry about. It stays put in the outlet. Offered in several versions (Type C, Type E/F, Type G), this adapter enables you to charge up to six gadgets. I’ve been testing the Type G model in Scotland, and it plugs into a single outlet, giving you three US outlets, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. The USB-C can output up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports are limited to 12 watts—not especially speedy, but fine for overnight charging. The adapter is grounded and has various safety features.

On the downside, it can be tough to use all the outlets simultaneously, as larger plugs, like the MacBook power adapter, tend to block one of the other US outlets. It does not offer surge protection, and the Type G adapter maxes out at 3,250 watts (250 volts, 13 amps), while the EU and other versions top out at 2,500 watts.

If you only need USB-C and USB-A ports for charging your mobile gadgets on the go (and no outlet), I recommend this clever, compact travel adapter. I’ve never seen a mechanism like this before, where you twist to extend the prongs. It's a neat feature. The standard US prongs can be angled for Australia, and there are EU and UK prongs (types A, C, G, and I). The USB-C ports can deliver up to 70 watts, enough to charge a laptop (slowly), and there’s a USB-A port. You could charge up to three devices at once, though the wattage is divided between them, and it got a little warm when I did this. It uses gallium nitride (GaN) technology to keep the size down. This is a new brand to me, but I’ve been testing it on various devices for the last two weeks, and so far, so good.

Recent findings suggest that universal adapters don't always work properly everywhere, and most don’t have grounding. The cheaper and more reliable alternative is to buy individual adapters. The 12-piece international set from Ceptics is my favorite. It includes types to cover most of the globe, and each is properly grounded. Only visiting a single destination? Just pack the relevant type. These adapters don't have USB ports, so you’ll need the respective charging adapter for your gadgets.

In a recent development, this set is especially good for Europe because it includes Type C, E/F, and G adapters, so you’re covered for any socket. Ceptics offers an even cheaper and smaller five-piece set, but I don’t recommend it. The adapters are flimsy, there’s no grounding, and the European plug’s design doesn’t work well with the recessed sockets you will sometimes encounter. The drawback of plug adapters is that they’re easy to lose, but at least Ceptics includes a small bag for storage.

This kit includes multiple plug attachments that slide and lock into place to keep you powered across most of the world. It is bulky and much bigger than the average adapter but provides two grounded US AC outlets. There is also a built-in USB-C cable, two USB-A ports, and two USB-C ports. The USB-A ports and built-in USB-C cable offer a combined maximum charging rate of 15 watts. The USB-C ports support Power Delivery, with up to 20 watts each. The top charging rate for all of them simultaneously is 55 watts.

In a recent development, there is built-in surge protection, but since this is not a voltage converter, don’t plug in hair dryers or other non-dual-voltage electronics. While the two AC outlets are handy, their proximity means that the shape and size of some plugs can make it tricky to use both simultaneously. But with the ability to charge up to seven devices, this kit is handy. I also like the original Ceptics World Travel Adapter Kit ($35), though it lacks the two USB-C ports.

Recent findings suggest that this cute kit comes in a zippered pouch and includes everything you need for a trip. There’s a fold-out charger with a tiltable magnetic Qi2 25W pad for your iPhone or Qi2 Android phone, a 7.5W pad for an Apple Watch, and a 5W pad behind for wireless earbuds. It also includes a 40W power adapter with switchable plugs for the US, UK, EU, and AU—plus a 5-foot USB-C cable. Everything inside comes in color-matched black or cream, unless you opt for the bolder orange-and-teal special edition.

Industry observers note that it’s not the most compact option, but I love that everything slots neatly into the included pouch. You can find some great alternatives in my Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers guide.

What Type of Adapter Do You Need?

Industry observers note that there are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.

It has been revealed that some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India (Type D), Israel (Type H), and South Africa (Type M or N). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.

If you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.

Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?

Voltage converters are big, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:.

Sources indicate that that should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. Most places provide hair dryers, irons, and kettles, so there’s no need to take them with you. It’s also often cheaper to buy a set with the correct plug at your destination and save the luggage space and hassle.

If you are determined to try a voltage converter (again, I don’t recommend doing so), the Ceptics 2,000-watt Travel Voltage Converter ($70) seems to work well. It has a special 2,000-watt outlet for hair dryers, but only ones that work via a mechanical switch (anything with an electronic circuit board for automatic switch-off or temperature control won’t work and is at risk of being fried if plugged in). It also has two outlets that go up to 200 watts, one USB-C port, and three USB-A ports, though the ports do not support fast charging.

In a recent development, travel adapters and chargers usually state the wattage they can deliver for USB-C and USB-A ports, retractable cables, and wireless charging. If you're interested in getting the fastest rates possible, you’ll want a charger and cable that can deliver the maximum wattage to your device. A laptop might want 100 watts, while a phone only needs 30 watts. There's no need to worry if the charger can deliver more wattage than is required because the device will dictate how much power to draw. If the wattage is lower than required, most devices will simply charge slowly. You can find out more about charging standards like Power Delivery (PD), Quick Charge (QC), and others in my guide on how to fast charge your phone.

Can Travel Adapters Go in a Suitcase?

In a recent development, yes, you can pack travel adapters in your suitcase. It may be wise to bring one in your hand luggage for easy access should you need to charge up a device when you arrive at your destination. In fact, devices like power banks with lithium batteries (must be capped at 27,000 mAh) must go in hand luggage, not checked bags.

Can I Buy Travel Adapters at the Airport or Hotel?

You certainly can buy travel adapters at the airport, but like all other goods you buy at kiosks between connecting flights, they will be far more expensive than necessary, and your choice will be limited.

In a recent development, some hotels have travel adapters, and some even have wall outlets for other countries (or USB-A and USB-C ports), but most do not, so don’t bank on it. You can always check with your hotel or accommodation before you depart, but it’s safer to bring a travel adapter with you.

Should You Test Your Travel Adapter Before You Go?

Seriously, nothing is worse than thinking you’re being very clever by packing light only to get to your hotel and discover that your gadgets refuse to charge. Between the adapter, cable, and your device, plenty can go wrong, so do a quick test on your wall outlet at home with everything you are taking before you set off on an international trip.

Anytime I fly for work or vacation, I take a few travel adapters and chargers with me to test. I also test them for longer periods at home in the UK. I have power stations and power strips with US and EU outlets to test those plugs. I test each charger with a variety of devices (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, MacBook, AirPods). I try charging with every port and outlet simultaneously to see if the charger gets warm. I assess the charging rates, durability, size, weight, and usability of each device. If there are any special features, I test them too.

It has been revealed that there is an endless amount of travel adapters out there you could buy. While I wholeheartedly recommend one of the options above, there are some other travel adapters I've tested that just barely miss the mark.

The sliders work well and lock in place securely to cover you in around 200 countries. A pair of USB-C and two USB-A ports provide a good mix of port options. Latest Update: Potty-mouthed MPs ranked as Australian parliament sets new swearing record

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One serial swearing offender, Jacqui Lambie, says it wouldn’t be an Australian parliament ‘without a few swear words thrown in’.
  • When Liberal MP Garth Hamilton stormed out of parliament in June, slamming his hands on his desk and calling out “fucking bullshit”, the speaker of the house, Milton Dick, called it “a latest low” in federal politics.
  • Newly introduced analysis from Guardian Australia has found profanity and foul language has risen significantly in Australia’s parliament over the past 20 years, with some of today’s most prominent politicians among the chief culprits for swearing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One serial swearing offender, Jacqui Lambie, says it wouldn’t be an Australian parliament ‘without a few swear words thrown in’.

When Liberal MP Garth Hamilton stormed out of parliament in June, slamming his hands on his desk and calling out “fucking bullshit”, the speaker of the house, Milton Dick, called it “a latest low” in federal politics.

Dick may have been on to something.

Newly introduced analysis from Guardian Australia has found profanity and foul language has risen significantly in Australia’s parliament over the past 20 years, with some of today’s most prominent politicians among the chief culprits for swearing.

Before the year is even out, 2026 is the worst year on record for the use of swear words and language deemed “unparliamentary”. That number has risen by 78% since 2006.

Analysis of Hansard debate and procedure records has found that per million words spoken in parliament this year, approximately 37 have been profane – ranging from milder (“bloody”, “damn” and “crap”) to language considered strong, or even extreme.

While entitled to “parle hard”, language deemed unparliamentary by the speaker or Senate president is required to be withdrawn, or else MPs face ejection from the chamber.

Beyond the impact of pushing against regulation and etiquette, there is something to be remarked for the currency that outbursts gain when clipped and shared online – recently demonstrated by Greens senator Peter Whish-Wilson, who called for the country to “wake the fuck up” to One Nation’s use of social media algorithms in June.

But despite the politicians reaching for profanities at a record rate, Dick – the Labor MP who has been speaker of the house since 2022 – said he felt the tone and tenor of debate in parliament has gotten better in his time in the chair.

“Debate is fierce and strong and, apart from a few incidents, it has improved,” he said.

“Maybe it hasn’t appeared so because of the volume [of swearing], but when you analyse the words used … there are outbreaks of course, but I believe in everyone showing respect.”.

And, to be fair, most of parliament’s most swear-y politicians are in the Senate, not the house.

Industry observers note that described as “the great Australian adjective” in 1894 by the Bulletin magazine, “bloody” appears to have suffered no fall from grace in the subsequent years, serving as the most commonly used swear word in parliament. Along with “damn”, “crap” and “bugger”, mild curses constitute 92% of all recorded bad language, with more severe terms such as “prick”, “shit” and “piss” used more sparingly.

Recent findings suggest that excluded from this figure are rare cases of colourful and creative terms that have been called for withdrawal. Harnessing the speaker’s unilateral power to flag unacceptable language, terms such as “bin chickens – used by Julian Hill, the MP for Bruce, in 2022 to describe the opposition in the house – have been ruled as unparliamentary.

Recent findings suggest that much of this potty-talk comes from the Senate, which since 2006 has seen a 177% increase in the use of bad language. Among active parliamentary participants (those who have spoken at least 100,000 words in this period), Bill Heffernan was the lead offender. Despite speaking just 141,000 words between 2006 and 2016, the former Liberal senator had an expletive use-rate of 877 per million words spoken, 43 times the rate of all other parliamentarians.

It has been revealed that jacqui Lambie is the second-most sweary politician, responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament at a rate of 406 per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. But, like most of the politicians on this list, Lambie’s swearing is overwhelmingly mild – mostly words like “crap” or “bloody”.

According to recent reports, “I try really hard not to swear, especially in the Senate chamber. It upsets my mum, she doesn’t even like me saying ‘bloody’,” Lambie said when we came to her with the statistics.

It has been revealed that “It’s important to be respectful. But I am a straight shooter and sometimes things are just crap – and it’s hard not to say so. I don’t think it would be an Australian parliament without a few swear words thrown in.”.

According to recent reports, not all occurrences of swearing in parliamentary records are “own-use” or, rather, swearing with intent. Quotes, such as reading out abuse a politician has received, or a quote from a document, account for some of it.

However, when excluding these cases our analysis indicates that own-use swearing in parliament has nearly tripled over the last 20 years, from 6.4 per million words in 2006-9 to 18.9 in 2022-5.

Broken down by party, One Nation are the worst offenders, swearing for the sake of it at 7.4 times the rate of Labor – perhaps unsurprising, given that the party leader, Pauline Hanson, ranks fourth among discursively active politicians for use of foul language.

Dick said he had strived to improve the tone of discussion in parliament, believing that greater diversity in politics and in the chamber – with more women, more First Nations MPs and people from multicultural backgrounds – had also changed dynamics of debate.

Asked about recent heated moments in parliament, he said he recalled only two major moments in the lower house in recent years: Hamilton’s June storm-out and fellow Liberal MP Dan Tehan’s demand to “cut the crap” in August.

“I want to ensure, among our people and our democracy, that we fight hard to disagree more civilly … But I’m a substantial believer in upholding traditions and standards. When things get a bit heated, I’ll take firm action,” Dick stated.

In a recent development, politicians’ speeches from both houses of parliament were analysed for the years 2006 to 2026. For each speech, the number of swearwords were counted using the these categories:.

Mild: bloody, damn, crap, bugger, bastard, bulldust, arse, mongrel, boofhead, bollocks.

Strong: prick, shit, bullshit, piss, piss off, dickhead, arsehole, shithouse, wanker.

Extreme: fucking, cunt, fuck, fuck off, fucker, fucked, motherfucker.

To control for politicians’ tenure length and verbosity affecting swearing totals, swearing numbers were converted to a rate per million words by dividing the total swearwords by the total number of words spoken for that politician in that year, or for the total time period.

To separate swearing in a politician’s own voice from quotes, idioms and literal uses, an LLM was used to read the speech text surrounding each swearword and sort these into categories. A random sample of the results were manually checked, to achieve an agreement of 97% on whether a use was the speaker’s own. Therefore these figures are approximate.

#116026. Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded

Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a newly introduced Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025.
  • Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.

Recent findings suggest that in a newly introduced Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it’s really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”.

Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.

It has been revealed that karambelkar’s team spotted a candidate system where this might be happening while searching Andromeda for stars changing in brightness, using the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) telescope at Palomar Observatory and data from NASA’s Near-Earth Object Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (NEOWISE) mission. One giant had been brightening for seven years. “When a star first swallows its companion, it has a very subtle effect on its brightness,” Karambelkar noted. “It slowly brightens, and a lot of light comes out in the infrared.”.

In April 2025, Karambelkar’s team published a paper suggesting that this system, named AT 2025abao, was undergoing an engulfment in progress. Back then, though, they couldn’t rule out a competing explanation: a single star with instabilities deep within its core. So, they kept watching.

It has been revealed that the researchers reconstructed the history of the system using observations from about a dozen telescopes and surveys, going back to photographic sky plates from 1989. Until 2018, the star barely changed. Modeling those quiet years revealed a giant late in its life, about 350 times wider than the Sun. Its companion was impossible to see, however. “The giant star outshines the smaller star by a factor of about 18,000,” Karambelkar said.

It has been revealed that to get around it, the team estimated the mass of the smaller companion based on the amount of dust the system had shed before the engulfment. The estimates suggested a star of roughly 0.7 solar masses.

Between 2018 and early 2025, the giant brightened two- to threefold in visible light, swelling while its temperature stayed nearly constant. Karambelkar compares the process to a spacecraft reentering Earth’s atmosphere. The companion, skimming through the giant’s outer layers, was gradually seeing its orbit shrink, and the friction was heating up the envelope. The energy released by that drag matched the extra light the team observed.

Then, the star’s visible light dropped by half while its infrared glow kept rising. NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope happened to catch it in July 2025, revealing that the giant had swollen to some 860 times the Sun’s width and wrapped itself in fresh dust.

It has been revealed that in October 2025, the star brightened roughly 100-fold in just 25 days, shining like 1.5 million Suns at its peak. “At one point, the rate at which the orbit was decaying became very, very fast,” Karambelkar said, comparing the release of the gravitational energy to an explosion. “The companion just fell very rapidly, very deep inside the envelope of the star, and it crashed into the core. That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star, and that explosion caused it to brighten very quickly and eject some of the material.”.

Sources indicate that the eruption had all the hallmarks of a luminous red nova, a type of outburst known to come from merging stars—but an event the researchers weren’t expecting. “Honestly, our minds were blown,” Karambelkar mentioned. He said that this was evidence that this explosion was a consequence of the inspiraling of a binary companion. What made AT 2025abao special, though, was the giant itself.

All previously known luminous red novae came from younger stars with dense, tightly bound outer layers, which inevitably drive both stars toward a merger. This one was an old giant with a loose, churning envelope—the setup that can also leave behind a surviving tight binary. To find out if the companion actually survived, the team looked at how AT 2025abao’s energy was spent.

Industry observers note that to predict how such events end, astronomers use a formula with an efficiency parameter describing how much of the energy lost by the sinking companion goes into blowing the envelope away. AT 2025abao revealed that the energy goes to different places at different stages.

Recent findings suggest that during the slow spiral, most of the energy escaped as light. In the final plunge, the companion released about a hundred times more energy, but only around 1 percent of it was radiated away. Nearly all the rest went into hurling a tenth of the envelope outward at about 10 times the speed needed to escape the giant’s gravity. The rest of the envelope stayed put, which suggests the companion merged with the giant’s core instead of surviving as a tight partner.

“Initially, when the rate of energy deposition is low, the star is able to puff up and adjust to this latest energy source inside it,” Karambelkar mentioned. “But once the energy deposition rate increases very promptly as the companion spirals even closer, the star can no longer adjust itself. At that point, it needs to throw out some of its material.”.

According to recent reports, the efficiency the team calculated fits values inferred from known post-engulfment binaries. But the formula assumes the energy is mostly spent expelling lots of the envelope. Here, most of it went into flinging a small amount of gas at high speeds. It turned out the formula works as a rule of thumb but misses some of the physics.

Recent findings suggest that in AT 2025abao, gas shed during the slow spiral piled up in the plane of the binary’s orbit, so the explosion’s ejecta could expand freely toward the poles even though it was blocked around the equator. That, Karambelkar argues, explains the hourglass-shaped nebulae seen around dying stars. “It had been an idea for a very long time that those hourglass shapes are shaped by binary interactions,” he remarked. “It seems like what we’re seeing here confirms that hypothesis.”.

Industry observers note that the team admits it can’t yet be sure the stars merged, because dust formed from the ejected material hides whatever is left inside. “We want to continue monitoring the system for several years, possibly even decades, to watch the dust clear out and whatever is remaining inside emerge,” Karambelkar noted. “That will conclusively tell us whether this merged or the binary system survived.” In the meantime, the team hopes to find many more such events involving stars of different masses and types.

Recent findings suggest that telescopes we have today can detect them only as far as Andromeda, but the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should spot them in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within some 50 million light-years. “We can have an influx of several of these events per year,” Karambelkar mentioned.

Sources indicate that nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z.
