Latest Update: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.
  • But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health complications – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.
  • Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.

But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health complications – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.

Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.

Since then, the 23-year-old has been battling to recover not only from that injury but also with a debilitating neurological condition diagnosed as "absence seizures" which led him to collapse on the pitch in two consecutive pre-season games in August this year.

Musiala has struggled to replicate the sort of form which led to a well-remunerated contract extension in January 2025, prior to the ankle injury and the seizures.

And on Sunday morning, German media including tabloid BILD and broadcaster Sport1 reported that Musiala had suffered another seizure as recently as last Monday, believed to be a result of an adjustment to his medication.

Musiala was deemed fit to feature against Cologne on Friday but the most recent incident prompted a series of controversial public remarks from the Bayern hierarchy seemingly questioning the validity of that contract.

"It is well known that he has a contract which contains some considerable sums," former chief executive and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told broadcaster Sky on Friday evening following the 1-1 draw with Cologne, in which Musiala had made a 20-minute substitute appearance.

"It's in all of our interest that he comes back, ideally in top form, but what happens if that's not the case?" asked Rummenigge, adding that Musiala's condition "leads us to suspect, unfortunately, that it will be difficult [for him] to return to the level that he has often shown in this stadium" and that "then we of course have to think about the finances.".

Rummenigge suggested a need for Bayern to hold talks with Musiala, his family and his representatives because "such sums are, with respect, no longer justifiable.".

Asked whether Bayern would consider selling Musiala, Rummenigge mentioned he considered it unlikely that any club would be prepared to buy the player out of his new contract, which is set to run until 2030 and which reportedly sees Musiala earn up to €30 million per year.

It has been revealed that "I cannot imagine that Jamal would leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions," said Rummenigge. "And that is a problem.".

Recent findings suggest that rummenigge was not the first senior Bayern official to express such doubts. Earlier this month, former club president Uli Hoeness had told local broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk that Musiala's situation presented the club with a "dilemma.".

"He has an illness which cannot be cured but which can be somewhat controlled through medication," noted Hoeness, who also sits on Bayern's supervisory board, questioning "whether he will ever regain the ability he once had" and stating that "he continues to receive money.".

Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen has also weighed in, telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper last week: "We all have a responsibility towards the club and we all hope that Jamal will come back. Of course this will take time. We will assess the situation and speak to his family and management. Either we'll all be happy that the old Jamal [will return] or, if he becomes a different [player], we'll have to hold talks.".

The comments by Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge landed like a bombshell in Germany and beyond.

The global players' union FIFPRO issued a statement on Saturday slamming what they called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations," highlighting Bayern's "duty of care" towards their player, and stating: "A club of Bayern's standing should know better.".

Industry observers note that "Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury," the statement continued. "Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise.".

Former Bayern Munich and Germany defender Lothar Matthäus also criticized the club, saying in his role as a pundit for Sky: "I've been a bit shocked throughout the entire week. It started with Uli Hoeness, continued with Jan-Christian Dreesen, and yesterday Karl-Heinz Rummenigge chose the strongest words of all. I have enormous respect for Karl-Heinz. I've known him for over 30 years. But he chose those statements very deliberately. The person who suffers most from all this is Jamal Musiala.".

The comments by the Bayern bosses also came just hours ahead of the club's annual general meeting on Saturday, where club members – who hold a majority 70% stake in the club in accordance with German football's "50+1" ownership rule – took to the stand to criticize the club's hierarchy.

One member, professional neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, expressed his "absolute respect" for Musiala and noted that patients suffering from such conditions require "support.".

He stated Musiala had received such support from head coach Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl, but said Hoeness', Dreesen's and Rummenigge's comments were "not helpful" and had "little to do with the much talked about Bayern Munich family" – earning considerable applause from fellow members.

Bayern president Herbert Hainer, the club's most senior elected official, attempted to deescalate the situation, responding to Hoffmann by saying: "Health and difficult situations are fundamentally always taken into account at FC Bayern.".

Indeed, Bayern have recently been praised for their considerate handling of captain Joshua Kimmich following the unexpected death of his father, and of head coach Kompany, who returned to the touchline against Cologne on Friday following a month-long absence after collapsing due to a particularly serious viral infection.

"When it comes to Jamal, we all want the old Jamal back as he was before his injury," stated Hainer. "And he will receive all the support and time he needs from the club.".

Speaking on the sidelines of the meeting, chief executive Dreesen also attempted to row back on his comments, insisting to reporters that he and his colleagues had not been trying to put Musiala under pressure.

It has been revealed that "We all want Jamal to return to the old Jamal. He needs time. We've said that several times. And he must get that. And then we'll see how things look in the new year," he said, adding that there was no need "to talk about the contract.".

President Hainer also dismissed questions from journalists as to whether Bayern felt they had been misled by Musiala's agents before offering him a fresh contract, inferring that the player's representatives may have known about his neurological condition.

"I absolutely do not think that anyone knew beforehand," Hainer insisted.

It has been revealed that but the public criticism has continued. Leading German sports publication Kicker remarked it was understandable for the Bayern bosses to be frustrated but called their approach "irresponsible" and said their anger "harms the wrong person" in Musiala.

It has been revealed that "He can't help his injuries or neurological condition," wrote editor-in-chief Matthias Dersch. "Musiala is only 23 … and is in the most difficult phase of his career. We cannot imagine how he must be feeling, his insecurities and perhaps also fears about his health and his future. And no: the amount of money he earns is no cure.".

German football magazine 11Freunde said the Musiala case offered "a glimpse into the abyss of professional football … an unembellished look behind the scenes of a business which is generally portrayed only as glamorous and exciting … into a shadow world where human beings are damned to function … where the value of a person is measured only by their ability to perform over and over again … That's football: capitalism in its purest form.".

Meanwhile, the business of football continues. Borussia Dortmund capitalized on Bayern's draw to go top of the Bundesliga with a 1-0 win away at Borussia Mönchengladbach, Harry Kane underwent an operation on a torn ankle ligament but will be out until the fresh year, meaning he will miss Bayern's trip to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.

And the young Jamal Musiala will continue to battle the effects of serious physical and neurological conditions.

You don't need a foldable phone to use split screen on Android

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that despite all odds, folding smartphones have stuck around.
  • In a recent development, split screen multitasking has been around since Android 7.0 Nougat, which was released a decade ago in 2016.
  • Recent findings suggest that this can be accessed by swiping up from the very bottom and holding on the screen if you're using gesture navigation, or by tapping the Recents button if you use the three-button navigation system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slab-style phones can do this trick too.

Recent findings suggest that despite all odds, folding smartphones have stuck around. They've mostly found their place in two  categories: flip phones that fold a regular-sized smartphone in half for portability and book-style phones that unfold to reveal a larger canvas. For years, foldables like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 have been marketed as productivity machines, allowing you to get more things done on a device you carry around in your pocket. Split screen multitasking is often highlighted as one of their biggest selling points, but you don't need to set aside close to $2,000 just to use two apps at the same time.

In a recent development, split screen multitasking has been around since Android 7.0 Nougat, which was released a decade ago in 2016. In fact, the feature was first discovered in Android 6.0 Marshmallow, though it required root access. All modern Android smartphones should come with this multitasking feature out of the box, but the exact steps to activate it might differ depending on your phone's manufacturer and Android version. Most phones, including ones from Google, Samsung and Motorola, let you enable split screen multitasking through the recent apps switcher.

Recent findings suggest that this can be accessed by swiping up from the very bottom and holding on the screen if you're using gesture navigation, or by tapping the Recents button if you use the three-button navigation system. All of your opened apps will be listed here. Tap on an app's icon and select Split Screen from the options that show up. You can now select a second app that you want open alongside the first one. You can further adjust how much space each app occupies by dragging the divider in the middle. Dragging it all the way up or down will exit the split screen mode.

It has been revealed that most traditional slab-style Android phones only let you use a maximum of two apps at once in split screen view — not that you'd realistically want to cram a third one onto such a small display anyway. This is where larger foldables let you take multitasking a step further by accommodating three or more apps at the same time. That said, split screen view isn't the only multitasking feature that Android offers.

Sources indicate that modern Android phones also let you use apps in floating windows, which allows for a slightly different kind of multitasking. Instead of splitting your screen in two halves, a floating window appears on top of whatever app you're currently using. This lets you view and interact with two apps simultaneously without splitting the screen. You can move the floating window around or resize it by grabbing its edges or corners.

Industry observers note that different manufacturers handle this feature differently. Pixel phones running Android 17, for instance, offer the Bubbles feature, which lets you use floating apps that collapse into Facebook Messenger-style chat heads when minimized, allowing you to open them swiftly without leaving your current app. Samsung calls this feature Pop-up view while some manufacturers like OnePlus and Oppo simply label it Floating Windows.

Recent findings suggest that colorOS 17 handles it particularly well, even allowing you to change the aspect ratio of certain floating windows. My OnePlus 15 can accommodate two apps in split screen view and a third one running in a floating window on top, though I'm yet to find a use case that warrants this level of multitasking madness on a slab-style phone.

Though the feature has been around for a hot minute, you may find the split view mode not working in some cases. App compatibility has improved a lot over the years, but there are still a few apps that might not work in multiwindow setups. When this is the case, you'll either find the Split View option greyed out or simply missing. It's still worth heading to the Play Store and updating all of your apps to see if an app's newer version might introduce support for split screen multitasking.

If not, this is Android we're talking about, so of course there's a workaround. Hidden away in the Developer Options menu is the Force activities to be resizable toggle. Turning this on might let you force split screen mode for apps that don't officially support it. This might not always work, though. For instance, it seemed to do the trick for all unsupported apps on my older Android phone, but I didn't have the same luck on my current device. There's also no guarantee that unsupported apps will play nicely in split screen view.

Industry observers note that the Developer Options menu is hidden by default. To enable it, navigate to Settings > About, look for the Build Number entry and tap on it seven times. Enter your PIN or password when prompted. Once enabled, you can find the hidden menu under Settings > System on most phones. While simply having Developer Options enabled isn't inherently dangerous, it does hold many advanced settings that might affect your phone's performance and stability, so it's best to leave anything you're not familiar with unchanged.

Transparency International claims Queensland’s David Crisafulli was ‘by far the most frequently accessed’ state leader, with 13 meetings.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

Bosses at 10 datacentre companies secured almost 120 meetings with premiers and ministers in five states over a three-year period, with experts declaring this is “just the tip of the iceberg”.

Analysis by Transparency International Australia argues these meetings, when combined with political donations, demonstrate “unfettered access” to decision-makers that creates an “uneven playing field”.

The report found donations from major datacentre companies and their contracted lobbying firms nearly tripled over the past three years from $685,000 to $1.8m, coinciding with increased investment across Australia.

The analysis found the Queensland leader, David Crisafulli, was “by far the most frequently accessed state premier”, with public diaries showing he has met datacentre executives 13 times in the past three years.

This included three meetings in as many weeks in August and September with Australia’s largest datacentre operator, NextDC – roughly one month before the company’s expansion in Melbourne was halted after its power provider delayed construction of new power poles due to community backlash.

“Those meetings took place shortly before the Queensland premier revealed a dedicated framework to fast-track datacentre approvals by taking them out of the hands of local councils,” the Transparency International report noted.

Crisafulli has embraced datacentre investment and flew to the United States in September to secure a $31.9bn deal with the AI giant Anthropic for what could become Australia’s largest datacentre. His office was contacted for comment.

It has been revealed that during this three-year period, 119 meetings with ministers or premiers were held in Latest South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, Queensland and the ACT. These are the only jurisdictions to publicly release ministerial diaries. The meetings were mostly held in 2026.

“These numbers are just the tip of the iceberg,” remarked Clancy Moore, the chief executive of Transparency International Australia.

“What we don’t know is how many meetings companies like NextDC, OpenAI and Anthropic and their third-party lobbyists are having with the prime minister and ministers in our federal parliament.

“Australia’s lobbying laws also don’t cover in-house lobbyists or government relations staff so there’s very little oversight of their activities too.”.

Industry observers note that the report also found Australian firm Firmus Technologies secured 10 meetings with Tasmanian ministers and the premier this year alone. During this period, the company’s expansion in the state has faced sustained backlash from local communities who feel they were not properly consulted.

The three companies that secured the most meetings with ministers were Amazon Web Services, Macquarie Technology Group and NextDC.

It has been revealed that last month, Guardian Australia reported on political donations from Amazon and Macquarie to both major parties, closely aligning with the announcement of multimillion-dollar government contracts or planning developments. Both companies say these donations were not aimed at influencing policy and that their timing was coincidental.

A shareholder at NextDC’s annual general meeting on Friday noted the tech giant had “a lot of lobbying going on in Canberra” but called on the company to better lobby the public on the benefits of datacentres.

The company’s chair, Stephen Flynn, stated he was “not sure we are great at lobbying as an industry or as a company” but the world had now changed.

“We thought we were just going along and [being] invisible, in the way if you think about all telecommunications systems … [it] is kind of invisible. We just take it for granted. But we can’t do that. We can’t do that as we go forward.”.

The report has also cited examples of four senior public servants at federal government departments quitting to assume leadership positions at OpenAI, AirTrunk and CDC. Three of these appointments were made this year.

In September, the president of the Australian Professional Government Relations Association, Sally Mackenzie, mentioned the scale of engagement between industry and ministers was a sign of the system working as intended.

“What we’re seeing with AI and datacentres is that dynamic playing out at real pace, because the stakes for industry, government and Australians more broadly are so high,” Mackenzie said.

According to recent reports, “Lobbying is an important part of the democratic process. It ensures that all stakeholders have the ability to communicate with government.”.

  • Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
  • The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific concerns that worried investors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?

Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific concerns that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

Sources indicate that the S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) manufacturer's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the firm was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI manufacturer experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he remarked.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability.".

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

It has been revealed that musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the manufacturer said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

But tech stocks more broadly also fell.

Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

#116013. Latest Update: What the tiny key icon means on your Android device

Latest Update: What the tiny key icon means on your Android device

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Android status bar is designed to give users important information at a glance, but all those icons can blur together.
  • It has been revealed that more specifically, that icon is a visual indicator that you're connected via a VPN that encrypts your web traffic from third parties.
  • In a recent development, if you use a VPN but don't want the key icon taking up space in your status bar, you're out of luck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Android status bar is designed to give users important information at a glance, but all those icons can blur together. One of the most unusual symbols looks like a leftward-facing key with two teeth opposite its circular handle. That icon tells you that your internet connection is encrypted, but there's nothing to worry about.

It has been revealed that more specifically, that icon is a visual indicator that you're connected via a VPN that encrypts your web traffic from third parties. Many people consider a VPN crucial for their online security, and modern Android versions support VPNs at the OS level. The key icon, then, lets owners know they're safe behind their VPN, while its absence alerts them that their encryption has been broken, giving them a chance to address it.

In a recent development, if you use a VPN but don't want the key icon taking up space in your status bar, you're out of luck. Because it's a security and privacy feature, most Android devices don't have a built-in option to remove the icon. Only Samsung Galaxy owners can do so, and even then, they'll need to download the Good Lock customization suite from the Galaxy Store and go into the QuickStar module to toggle the key indicator and other icons.

According to recent reports, the key icon appears only when a VPN is active, so the only way to get rid of it is to disable the VPN. If you're running a third-party VPN, open the app and turn it off from there. Some VPN apps even keep a notification active with a button to turn them off, making it an even quicker process. On a Pixel or other close-to-stock Android device, you can also swipe into Quick Settings and tap the number next to the profile icon at the bottom of the screen to show active background apps, then tap Stop next to your VPN.

If you don't know which VPN you're running, open your phone's Settings app and go to Network & internet > VPN, then tap on it from the list there. On Samsung Galaxy phones, go to Settings > Connections > More connection settings > VPN to find a functionally identical screen. If you are connected to a VPN, it will be shown on a list with text underneath reading "Connected." Tap the running VPN and choose Disconnect. If you are not connected to a VPN, tap a VPN, and you will be taken to its app, where you can connect.

Tapping the settings gear icon next to any VPN will allow you to configure it further. If you want to configure a VPN manually, you can tap the plus icon in the top right, but this is generally recommended for advanced consumers. For more, see our guide on how to use a VPN. All other aspects of your VPN can be managed within its proprietary app. Since every VPN has a different interface in its app, consult your provider's documentation if you're not sure how to use a feature or setting.

If you don't use a VPN, you may wonder whether it's worth installing one on your Android phone. How useful one will be depends largely on how privacy-minded you are, your streaming habits and whether you already have a VPN or need to get a subscription first.

It has been revealed that another classic use case is making it appear as though you are somewhere you're not, usually to access geofenced content. For instance, Netflix may offer shows in other countries that it doesn't in your own due to licensing deals, and a VPN will let you set your location to those regions to access that content.

While VPNs offer benefits, they can cause problems when browsing the web. Some websites will treat your device as inherently suspicious when it connects from a VPN IP address, and you may encounter more anti-automation measures such as CAPTCHAs. Some websites may even be totally unresponsive until you disconnect your VPN. Despite that, if you already pay for a service that includes a VPN, it may be worth enabling it to get a taste of what using a VPN is like on your phone. Otherwise, have a gander at our list of the best VPNs in 2026.

#116012. COP31: Climate deal 'not adopted,' summit president says

COP31: Climate deal 'not adopted,' summit president says

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement despite prolonging the talks.
  • The summit's president acknowledges that a deal was 'not adopted'.
  • The final draft presented at the summit in Antalya, Turkey omitted any mention of fossil fuels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement despite prolonging the talks.

The summit's president acknowledges that a deal was 'not adopted'.

The final draft presented at the summit in Antalya, Turkey omitted any mention of fossil fuels.

The EU states it cannot accept a deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels'.

Oil and gas consumption remains a major flashpoint amid soaring energy prices and tensions over the US-Israeli war with Iran.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was 'deeply disappointed' by the outcome.

These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22:.

It has been revealed that people from all over the world are suffering due to high prices of fossil fuels, Germany's Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the COP31 breakdown. He added that clean technologies such as electric vehicles, heat pumps and modernizing energy industries would free the people from this dependence.

It has been revealed that "I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," he remarked.

Previously, Schneider accused the oil and gas industry of dragging its feet on climate change, referencing the last-minute draft proposals which steered clear of fossil fuel phaseout.

"Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," Scheider said from Turkey.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Separately, the head of the German Environment Agency Dirk Messner stated the world was divided in two camps, with some countries focusing on averting climate change and others defending oil, coal, and natural gas.

"A fossil-fuel-based economy can quickly become obsolete if the majority of countries stand together," Messner noted.

Sources indicate that he urged the nations protecting the climate to continue boosting cooperation. At the same time, Messner warned that the world would not become climate-neutral by the middle of the century without nations like Russia, Saudi Arabia and the US all supporting this goal.

"This is why the global climate dialogue must continue," he remarked.

The EU's outright rejection to provide new finance commitments "set the tone" for the failed COP 31 climate summit, notes Tasneem Essop, executive director at the Climate Action Network, a group over 2,500 NGOs from various parts of the world.

Talking to DW from Turkey, Essop questioned the EU's narrative of rejecting the proposed agreement for not mentioning fossil fuels.

Essop remarked that the EU was pushing back and obstructing discussions dealing with the issues of the Global South.

"Rich nations are responsible for providing public finance to developing countries so that they can take climate action, so that they can transition away from fossil fuels," Essop noted.

"That requires financial support. And yet they came here without finance. So, it's left a bitter taste in many mouths about the action of rejection by the EU.".

Essop also pointed to the UK, Australia, and European countries granting additional licenses to obtain fossil fuels.

"You can't say you're rejecting something because of fossil fuels and yet in your practice and your actions back home, you're doing exactly the opposite," she stated.

She described the outcome of the summit, which went into overtime and then ended without an agreement, as "deeply disappointing.".

While oil producers like Saudi Arabia and Russia were criticized for blocking any mention fossil fuels in the draft COP31 declaration, one climate campaigner told DW that other wealthy countries also failed more vulnerable nations by not agreeing to a funded pathway for an energy transition.

Harjit Sing, strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative remarked developing nations had big ambitions to turn away from oil and gas, but needed resources to do so.

"If you look at Canada, the UK, Norway, not to mention the US, they continue to expand fossil fuels, yet they point fingers towards developing countries who have a large population," Sing told DW.

"But the reality is that [the developed countries] were the ones who were blocking the conversation and the progress that we needed to create a just transition mechanism.".

Sing remarked this lack of a funded strategy for developing countries was more urgent than whether or not the final declaration mentioned fossil fuels.

It has been revealed that "So not mentioning fossil fuels is just one part of it. The more important thing is we now need a blueprint, not repackaged national roadmaps, but a fair, fast and funded transition away from fossil fuels," he said.

"Fair: So rich countries move fast, [but] they are the ones who are historically responsible for the climate crisis. Fast, which is in line with science. And funded, so that developing countries get the right kind of support to make that shift.".

A combination of climate change effects and insufficient funding would be "a life or death scenario" for developing countries, Sing added.

"Even at one degree temperature rise, they were facing so many disasters and we are already going to breach that 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming," he stated.

After the failure of the COP31 summit over fossil fuels, Russia's delegate Sergey Kononuchenko argued that reducing the supply of oil without reducing the demand will cause "deficit, price shock and a switch to dirtier types of fuel" as well as "energy poverty," which will affect poorer countries first.

"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he mentioned.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's representative referred to a last-minute proposal that called for expanding carbon capture capacities.

"We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table," mentioned Mohammad Ayoub, speaking for the Arab Group of nations at the summit.

"It makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions... will be taken off the table.".

While capturing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is technically possible, critics say the technology is still in its infancy and lacks real-world infrastructure to move the needle on climate change.

Both Russia and Saudi Arabia had sought to omit any mention of fossil fuels in the final declaration, contributing the the impasse on Sunday.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres remarked he was "deeply disappointed" by the collapse of negotiations for a joint resolution at COP31.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," Guterres said in a statement.

According to recent reports, "There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science," he added.

In a recent development, "Those who profit from the destruction of our planet must never dictate the terms of the fight to save it," the UN chief remarked. "The continued addiction to coal, oil and gas is fueling climate chaos, exposing economies to price shocks, and undermining energy security," Guterres added.

Recent findings suggest that "Major emitters must lead. Developed countries must deliver on finance. And every country must do their part.".

Marshall Islands climate envoy Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner spoke out against fossil fuel interests after the conclusion of the summit with no deal.

Recent findings suggest that the Marshall Islands are a chain of volcanic atolls and coral islands numbering over 1,100 islands in total in the Pacific Ocean. Like many island nations, they are severly threatened by the effects of climate change on the earth's oceans.

Recent findings suggest that "We have been let down ​on all sides. We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a ⁠response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions," Jetnil-Kijiner said.

"We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future.".

Australian environment minister and COP31's president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, expressed disappointment that the sweeping deal he tried to broker ultimately collapsed.

As part of a compromise between the two countries, Turkey hosted the summit while Australia took a leading role over negotiations.

It has been revealed that "Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision... And that's disappointing. Very disappointing," said Bowen.

"An obvious glitch is the transition away from fossil fuels, where some parties insisted that must be mentioned, other parties insisted that if it was mentioned they would veto.".

Nevertheless, Bowen highlighted some of the ways in which the summit has still had a positive impact.

"A lot of good things happened this COP. A lot of events which told the clean energy story. A lot of commitments made — like the more than 90 countries that signed the electrification pledge, for example. And all that is good work and a great thing," he said.

The COP31 climate summit has failed to agree on a final joint declaration.

During a plenary session, the summit's Turkish president acknowledged there would be no climate deal.

According to recent reports, "I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, told a closing plenary in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.

In a recent development, the rift centered on whether to include the phaseout of fossil fuels in the final declaration. Scientists say the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas is the main cause of global warming.

European nations, smaller island states and climate activists have criticized oil-producing countries for the omission.

Several nations continued to raise serious objections to the draft.

Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, took a shot at the presidency for how it has handled the negotiations.

Recent findings suggest that "With all due respect Mr. President, you have not shown respect to a group of 54 countries (from Africa) and my country (Ghana) for that matter," Amoah noted.

Panama's representative noted the Central American nation was amongst those who suffer most from the consequences and issue of climate justice.

Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks were being held hostage by a "petroleum mafia" and need to be reformed.

He mentioned science must be the basis for the cover decision, adding that those who contributed to this crisis must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it.

Recent findings suggest that "We are running out of time," Navarro told attendees. "Panama cannot support this decision. The planet cannot continue to wait.".

Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien has said the European Union is "profoundly disappointed" with the current draft deal on the table at COP31 because it "fails to meet the moment" and that the bloc will not agree to it.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5°C within reach," O'Brien said.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels," he added.

Former Greenpeace executive Jennifer Morgan said it would be better to end the COP31 summit with no deal than a watered-down declaration.

Her remarks come amid deep divisions over the omission of fossil fuels from the draft declaration.

Morgan rejected the notion that it would be better to accept the current draft than have no resolution at all, as the Turkish COP president has suggested.

"I think this is the day for the first time in my 31 COPs that I thought it was better not to have a decision that sets us back, that goes against what small islands and vulnerable people are saying," Morgan added.

She praised Germany for standing up to pressures to accept the current deal.

"Of course it would have been better to have a strong outcome here with everyone moving forward, but I agree with the German minister who just stated if the text stays the way that it is, then it should not be accepted," Morgan said.

The US climate activist blamed oil-producing nations for the impasse.

"Saudi Arabia's fingerprints are all over" the current draft proposal, she mentioned.

The omission has created a deadlock at COP31, which was due to conclude on Friday but has been extended as delegates seek consensus.

Morgan also blamed this year's Turkish presidency for failing to bring everybody together and instead letting countries that rely on fossil fuels dictate the terms of the agreement.

"Last year we had Brazil with a very strong presidency. They worked all year to bring countries together and they managed. It was not easy last year," Morgan mentioned.

"This year we had presidencies that, in my view, were not well prepared. They did not bring countries together  (...) it's been shuttle diplomacy with no text for four days. That's not the way you get an agreement here," she added.

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider has remarked the latest version of the draft agreement is "not acceptable.".

Schneider mentioned that the draft decision "not only fails to provide an adequate response but actually takes a step backward. A step backward from previous decisions on climate protection is the last thing Germany can support.".

Schneider noted that delegates had been working hard for days to reach a unanimous decision on "the world's greatest challenge: human-induced climate change," noting that this summer had "shown that the nature of this warming not only costs lives — as in Nepal — but also changes our world for the worse.".

According to recent reports, "It is up to us, as humanity, to do something about it. That is why a conference dedicated to climate protection — whose sole purpose is to protect the climate — must send a clear signal that we are taking action against this threat.".

Schneider said he still believed most nations are willing to work to enact climate protection, but singled out those who still rely on fossil fuels to power their economies.

Sources indicate that "The overwhelming majority of nations are committed to climate protection. Some, however, are still making huge profits from oil and gas and are unwilling to scale back their production or to pioneer a clear roadmap for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in this area," he added.

France has called a latest draft deal proposed at COP31 a "backward" step.

French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut criticized the deal for failing to mention fossil fuels, casting fresh uncertainty over whether nations will be able to reach an agreement.

"Time is ticking and we are not there yet," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut stated in a statement.

COP31 President Murat Kurum has expressed his frustration over the deadlock at the summit.

The latest version of the draft deal again fails to mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

Over 40 hours after its scheduled conclusion and with no compromise in sight, the summit risks losing the numbers required to make any decision as delegates leave for home.

"If it is not adopted, I believe those who push the COP process into a deadlock will need to reflect on their position," Kurum noted.

"It is our wish that this resolution be passed. We shall shortly be expressing our determination to ensure that this resolution is passed at the general meeting," he remarked.

"It is up to the parties involved. If there is sincerity here, and if there is a genuine desire to get things done, I believe that this can be achieved in this chamber. We shall see about that in a moment," Kurum added.

#116011. Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1132 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them.
  • According to recent reports, the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does.
  • Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

According to recent reports, the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another massive provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and noted that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

According to recent reports, the findings are striking. They included:.

Industry observers note that “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”.

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:.

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

According to recent reports, secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were rapidly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

According to recent reports, last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:.

Sources indicate that the clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically highlighted up two or three days after the request.

Sources indicate that this wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

Recent findings suggest that the researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Australia’s climate change minister will face a torrent of criticism over his role, but disagreement over fossil fuels proved an unbridgeable sticking point.

After delivering a major speech to the UN climate talks in Turkey last week, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, dismissed criticisms that he hadn’t managed to name the problem that is overwhelmingly driving catastrophic global heating – burning fossil fuels.

“You could pick out any number of things that were not in what was a short speech,” he later remarked.

If Albanese really thought the head of a leading coal and gas exporter failing to address the issue head-on was inconsequential or trivial, then his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, will have a story for him after the finals days of the fractious talks that became the longest UN climate summit ever.

Those talks failed spectacularly to nail its prime ambition – an “Antalya pact” that was meant to drive investment in renewable energy and electrification, boost finance to help developing countries facing worsening climate damage, and acknowledge the world is bursting through a goal of limiting the increase in global temperatures to 1.5C, with alarming consequences across the planet.

As president of negotiations, Bowen barely slept for three days, and on the final night caught only a few moments of shut-eye on a couch in the office where a parade of negotiators had been coming to sit and talk to him.

It has been revealed that many of them raised a “red line” they stated was non-negotiable – that any agreement from the summit must refer to the need for the world to “transition away from fossil fuels” that had previously been agreed at talks in Dubai three years ago. Others, including Saudi Arabia, didn’t want the words “fossil fuels” mentioned at all.

A compromise was proposed in the two final drafts of what was meant to be a “cover decision” – an overarching agreement that all countries would back. Drawn up by Bowen and his verbose Turkish counterpart, Cop31 president Murat Kurum, it suggested countries would “recall” the decision in Dubai “in its entirety” – effectively acknowledge its existence – but not say fossil fuels directly.

Recent findings suggest that the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize were among the countries that mentioned no. Ireland’s climate minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the omission was “unconscionable” and the EU could not support it. Climate campaigners agreed.

With the scheduled Friday finish of the summit a distant memory, Bowen left the stage of the plenary hall late on Sunday afternoon when it was clear too many countries could not accept the text that he had helped put on the table.

Industry observers note that speaking to journalists, Bowen noted “Australia left nothing on the field” but the red lines he and his staff tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”. In particular, the way a transition away from fossil fuels was mentioned.

Some countries said they couldn’t support a pact that didn’t mention it, and others “insisted if it was mentioned, they would veto”. “I would have been happy with transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support,” Bowen said.

According to recent reports, bowen said despite the breakdown, “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and irreversible – and happening at speed. A promised electrification target – that 35% of final energy will come from electricity by 2035, a step that analysis has found could significantly cut fossil fuel use – had the backing of more than 90 countries and was not a deal-breaker.

Industry observers note that the climate minister will be presented with a torrent of criticism that the talks failed and he failed. Much domestic news coverage has focused on the cost of Cop31 to Australian taxpayers, rather than the substantive problems being dealt with.

It has been revealed that in Antalya, the narrative out of the talks was quite different. Some mentioned the rejection of the pact was a line in the sand that revealed the world was no longer willing to accept lukewarm responses on the climate crisis that bent to the whims of fossil fuel interests and petrostates. Some nations are setting up voluntary pacts outside the UN negotiations to try to get the results they need.

Industry observers note that despite some claims in the dramatic final hours, the talks did not actually collapse. Many less controversial elements of the convention’s myriad processes were passed.

Sources indicate that but the talks did fail to agree to the Antalya pact that Bowen and Kurum had spent so much political capital on. Some of this failure may be down to the Cop process itself – its reliance on consensus to pass agreements creates plenty of opportunities for countries to block and delay.

Luke Menzel, the chief executive of the Energy Efficiency Council, a membership group focused on electrification in Australia, was at the talks for the full two weeks. He notes the reality is “this process has been fracturing for a long time” and had become much tougher after years of wars, rising geopolitical tension and a fuel price crisis caused by conflict in Iran.

“It turns out Antalya is where the conference finally fractured. In many ways it is remarkable we have had as many Cops as we have had in a row that have achieved a consensus,” he says.

Many climate experts and high-profile figures were left questioning whether the Cop process needs major revision. The former US vice-president and long-time climate campaigner Al Gore was among them, arguing it was “an outrage” that “a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels” and concluding “it has been clear for years that the Cop process is in need of significant reform”.

Some campaigners sharply criticised Australia’s role. Denise Cauchi, the chief executive of Climate Action Network Australia, remarked it had “failed to broker an agreement” and “caved” to the hundreds of lobbyists that were pushing for controversial carbon capture and storage technology to be promoted in the pact. Its attempted inclusion was seen as a sop to fossil fuel interests.

But some from Pacific nations, who see the breach of the 1.5C temperature goal as existential and whose interests Bowen had promised to champion, noted the failure in Antalya is shared more widely.

In the chaotic final plenary session, the Fijian climate change minister, Lynda Tabuya, addressed Bowen directly as the rest of the world listened.

“You have tried your utmost best, and we have seen it. Your door has always been open,” she noted. “This work is hard – sleepless nights, and over hours and days of constant negotiations. This is not easy but we do it and we do it for our people.

“The failure here is not yours to carry. It is the responsibility of all parties.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
  • The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio.

Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

According to recent reports, lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

All were told they could never serve in the police again.

It has been revealed that the case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

The case was heard by a panel of five judges.

Recent findings suggest that the incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

According to recent reports, they later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

According to recent reports, after Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

According to recent reports, the officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

In a recent development, in their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

Macron 'shame' at police beating of black man.

Industry News: These iOS settings will help you control your mobile data use

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avoid data overage charges or speed thorttling with these iOS settings.
  • Sources indicate that cellular connectivity is now fast and reliable enough to rival home broadband, especially with 5G.
  • Recent findings suggest that the iPhone offers a handful of built-in settings that can help you monitor and manage mobile data use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Avoid data overage charges or speed thorttling with these iOS settings.

Sources indicate that cellular connectivity is now fast and reliable enough to rival home broadband, especially with 5G. But telcos typically aren't as generous about data allowances. If you don't watch your data use, you may end up with hefty bills — if your telco charges for excess data — or painfully slow speeds once you exceed your monthly allowance. You consume cellular data not just when you're downloading a file or watching a video, either: background app refresh, app updates and cloud syncing can also eat into your data allowance bit by bit.

Recent findings suggest that the iPhone offers a handful of built-in settings that can help you monitor and manage mobile data use. Firstly, you can view a list of apps and how much data they use by heading to Settings > Cellular, scrolling down to the Cellular Data section and tapping on Show All. This will list mobile data use for individual apps you have installed. You can sort these apps by name or usage to rapidly identify which ones consume the most data.

It has been revealed that tap the toggle next to any app to prevent it from using cellular data. The app will stop updating its content in the background when you're not connected to Wi-Fi and might also stop sending you notifications. The next time you launch the app, it will alert you that mobile data has been turned off for the app and give you the option to re-enable it.

If you rely mainly on Wi-Fi, turning off mobile data can prevent data usage and reduce battery drain. Navigate to Settings > Cellular to toggle Cellular Data on or off. iOS also lets you limit data consumption, so you can keep cellular data on without exhausting your monthly allowance as rapidly. In Cellular settings, navigate to Cellular Data Options > Data Mode and select Low Data Mode. This setting might be set to Standard by default, which allows automatic updates and background tasks even when you're not on Wi-Fi. Low Data Mode restricts this, reducing your mobile data use.

In a recent development, being connected to Wi-Fi doesn't guarantee that your iPhone won't consume mobile data. Head to Settings > Wi-Fi, scroll down and turn the Connectivity Assist toggle off. Before iOS 27, this feature was called Wi-Fi Assist and could be found under Settings > Cellular. The feature keeps your iPhone constantly connected to the internet, but it uses mobile data to do so. When a Wi-Fi connection becomes too weak or busy, Connectivity Assist switches to cellular data to keep you connected to the internet. If you don't mind potential disruptions, turning this feature off may reduce unexpected mobile data use.

Beyond the Settings app, there are other ways you can restrict mobile data use on your iPhone. For starters, changing automatic revision behavior can help avoid unexpected cellular activity. Navigate to Settings > Apps > App Store and, under the Mobile Data section, turn the Automatic Downloads toggle off. Open the Settings app, tap on your name at the top, navigate to iCloud > iCloud Backup and make sure the Back Up Over Mobile Data toggle is unchecked.

In a recent development, if you stream music regularly, check the audio quality in your app of choice. Apple Music customers can find this option by navigating to Settings > Apps > Music > Audio Quality > Data Streaming. Lossless audio may provide a superior listening experience, but it is an absolute data hog. Other apps, like Tidal, Spotify and YouTube Music, also let you reduce audio quality when using mobile data. Lowering video quality to 720p on YouTube can also help manage data consumption. You can also reduce how much data your navigation apps use by downloading maps for offline use; both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you do so.

Lastly, you can look for toggles and features in third-party apps designed to reduce cellular usage. For instance, you can stop WhatsApp from automatically downloading media from fresh chats by tapping your profile picture, navigating to Storage and data and setting the Media auto-download option for photos, videos and documents to Wi-Fi. Instagram fans can find a Use less mobile data toggle by opening the app's settings page and navigating to Media quality.

Breaking: How Secure Is Your Password? Here's How To Test It

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what a strong password looks like and how to check whether yours would hold up against hackers, plus a few habits that keep accounts safer.
  • According to recent reports, remember the old days when you'd try to use "1234" or "password" as your password?
  • It has been revealed that but even if you think you have created a password that Robert Langdon from The Da Vinci Code himself couldn't crack, how do you truly know how secure it is?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what a strong password looks like and how to check whether yours would hold up against hackers, plus a few habits that keep accounts safer.

According to recent reports, remember the old days when you'd try to use "1234" or "password" as your password? There really was never a time when passwords like those were secure. Thankfully, nowadays, most services don't even permit you to use passwords that aren't secure enough. They require a combination of letters, numbers and symbols along with different letter cases before accepting your chosen password. It makes passwords tougher to remember on the one hand, but it's essential in this day and age to ensure that your password can't be easily cracked by nefarious individuals or even AI systems.

It has been revealed that but even if you think you have created a password that Robert Langdon from The Da Vinci Code himself couldn't crack, how do you truly know how secure it is? Usually, if it includes all the elements noted above, especially if the letters do not connect to spell an actual word, you're in a good spot.

To know for sure, you can run it through a free password strength checker, such as the one at Security.org. However, remember that creating a secure password is just one of the steps you can take to be safer online.

Sources indicate that it's key to understand what makes a good password in the first place. It should be at least 12 characters, and in fact, many sites do not let you submit a password that is less than that anyway. Along with the aforementioned upper and lower case letters, numbers and symbols, keep in mind that the letters should not spell a discernible, and certainly not an identifiable word like your surname. They should also not be consecutive in the alphabet, like "LMNOP," or in a row on a keyboard, like "QWERTY." The same goes for numbers, which should be random instead of something like your birthday or street address. The letters and numbers should not be repeated as well, like "BBB" or "555.".

Once you create a password you think is secure, enter it into the Security.org checker, which evaluates it and provides feedback. As you type, the site indicates how long it would take a computer to crack the password. The more characters you add, the longer this duration becomes. I went from a password with letters and numbers that would take four years to figure out to one with symbols that bumps it to 2 million years before someone could crack it. It's safe to say both are secure, but the latter is more secure. When I tried using a simple word with consecutive numbers, it advised that the password could be cracked in three days.

When creating an account, you might see an option to "create a strong password" automatically after which you can save it to password memory, like Apple MacBook's Passwords app or a third-party password manager like 1Password. It's a good idea to use these even over signing in with an existing Google, Apple or other account. There are convenience benefits to doing that, but for extra security, create a fresh login.

It has been revealed that there are pros and cons of using a password manager over an authenticator app, but there's no reason you can't use both. If the site offers passkeys versus passwords, these are worth using. They can be more secure, relying on a private key accessed through biometrics (your fingerprint or face) or a PIN.

According to recent reports, along with having a secure password, it is also vital to make every password unique. If you use the same password for everything, no matter how secure, what happens if someone gains access to it from one account? This could happen through a breach or even human error, and it would unlock all your accounts and services. Keeping passwords secure and unique to every service and changing them every 60 to 90 days or immediately if a breach has been reported will keep you as safe as possible.
